Announced on October 27, the change begins on November 16, 2026, with Server Web Pages and discussion summaries. Individual messages will start rolling out in mid-December, not November, giving users and moderators […]

The post Discord to Make Discoverable Public Server Messages Searchable on Google appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Discord will make selected messages from Discoverable Servers searchable through Google and other search engines, opening some community discussions to the wider web.

Announced on October 27, the change begins on November 16, 2026, with Server Web Pages and discussion summaries. Individual messages will start rolling out in mid-December, not November, giving users and moderators time to review their privacy settings before posts become searchable.

According to Discord’s announcement, the aim is to make useful answers easier to find without first searching inside Discord. The company says knowledge shared in gaming guides, support discussions, and community forums often remains difficult for outsiders to reach.

Which Discord Messages Will Appear on Google?

The update applies only to Discoverable Servers, which anyone can find and join without an invitation. These communities must have at least 1,000 members, be eight weeks old, and meet activity and safety rules. Discord says more than 63,000 servers currently fall into this category. Private servers, direct messages, and group direct messages are excluded.

Every Discoverable Server will have a Server Web Page from November 16. Where moderators have not published one, Discord will create a default page using the Server Profile. Automated Channel Summaries may appear that day, covering discussions from November 16 onward.

Individual Channel Messages follow in mid-December through a gradual rollout. Only eligible messages sent from that point onward can appear. Older message histories will not be published through this feature. Usernames and avatars will be hidden, while messages will initially appear as text.

Discord’s member guidance says participating channels will display an icon and a notice before users post. Public threads and forums can qualify, but private threads and private forums remain excluded.

How Users Can Stop Their Messages Appearing

Users can open User Settings > Data & Privacy and disable “Show my message content from Discoverable channels on web pages.” This account-wide switch covers every Discoverable Server they belong to. Discord says the control can be changed through its desktop app or browser and applies across devices, including mobile.

The setting is enabled by default in most regions. It is disabled by default in the EU/EEA, UK, Canada, Brazil, Australia, and South Korea. Teen accounts are excluded and cannot enable the feature. Server and channel eligibility rules still apply even where a user’s setting is enabled.

Turning the switch off only protects messages sent afterward. Messages posted while it was enabled can still appear, even if they have not reached a web page yet. Users must delete those messages to remove them from Discord’s pages. Search engines may retain indexed or cached copies longer and require separate removal steps.

These controls address a planned publishing feature, not a security breach. That distinction separates this announcement from the earlier Discord customer support data breach, which involved unauthorized access through a third-party provider.

Moderators can manage participation through Server Settings > Web Presence. They can exclude selected channels or disable all channel participation. Without changes, public channels remain enabled. User opt-outs do not disable Channel Summaries, which have separate admin controls. Communities unwilling to maintain a Server Web Page can leave Discovery and remain Community Servers.

For security teams, the key concern is wider exposure rather than a newly disclosed flaw. Removing usernames does not remove identifying details written inside messages. Public support channels therefore deserve review before publication, particularly where members discuss workplace systems or share personal information.

Search visibility also should not be mistaken for proof of trust. Earlier reporting on expired Discord invite links used to spread malware showed attackers directing visitors into fake communities. Readers finding Discord answers through Google should check destinations and avoid running commands presented as account verification steps.

AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Torrance, United States / California, October 27th, 2026, CyberNewswire

AI SPERA, the company behind the cyber threat intelligence and attack surface management platform Criminal IP, has signed a cooperation agreement with the International Criminal Police Organization (INTERPOL) under its Gateway initiative. The agreement establishes a framework for sharing information and technical expertise relevant to cybercrime analysis.

Established in 2019, INTERPOL’s Gateway initiative provides a secure framework for sharing cyber threat intelligence with trusted private sector partners, including cybersecurity companies, technology providers and financial institutions. Partners can contribute indicators of compromise, insights into cybercriminal tactics and techniques, and threat analysis. INTERPOL reviews this information alongside other intelligence to develop investigative leads, which may be shared with member countries concerned by a threat.

Under the agreement, Criminal IP plans to contribute threat data, analysis and technical expertise to support INTERPOL’s cybercrime efforts. Criminal IP provides intelligence on IP addresses, domains and internet-exposed assets, helping analysts investigate suspicious infrastructure and identify connections between cyber threats. The cooperation aims to apply these capabilities to the development of intelligence relevant to cross-border investigations.

“Our participation in INTERPOL’s Gateway initiative marks a meaningful milestone for Criminal IP,” said Byungtak Kang, CEO of Criminal IP. “Cybercrime crosses borders, and effective investigations depend on timely intelligence and cooperation between the public and private sectors. We look forward to contributing our threat intelligence and technical expertise to this shared effort.”                                                                                                  

About Criminal IP

Criminal IP is a cyber threat intelligence solution operated by AI SPERA that provides decision-ready threat intelligence, and AI-powered threat exposure management solutions to security teams worldwide. By continuously scanning the global internet, Criminal IP aggregates and contextualizes threat signals across IPs, domains, URLs, and attack infrastructure, covering malicious indicators, known vulnerabilities, exposed assets, and attacker behavior.

Criminal IP’s mission is to give organizations real visibility into their cyber landscape and accelerate threat detection and response by delivering the intelligence needed to outsmart attackers. For more information, visit www.criminalip.io

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
What if some of the threats reaching your organization’s environment had already been identified elsewhere, before your security team even started investigating them? 

Chances are, some were. 

According to ANY.RUN’s research, up to 30% of unique malicious indicators of compromise (IOCs) identified in studied Interactive Sandbox sessions had already been observed by ANY.RUN and were present in its Threat Intelligence Feeds before investigation. 

In other words, nearly one in three of those malicious indicators was already available in threat intelligence before the analysts began their investigations. 

What does this mean for SOC teams, and how can they take advantage of threat data from investigations by 16,000+ security teams? 

What Does This Data Mean for Your SOC? 

Simply put, this means that your SOC can potentially recognize malicious indicators before analysts need to investigate them manually. 

If an indicator has already been associated with malicious activity elsewhere, that threat data can help your security systems identify suspicious events earlier and provide analysts with a starting point for early detection. 

For that, threat intelligence needs to reach the security systems your team already uses, in time to influence detection and response. That’s where integrated threat intelligence comes in. 

What’s Integrated Threat Intelligence and What Does It Bring to SOC Operations? 

Integrated threat intelligence, such as TI Feeds, doesn’t require major additions to your normal SOC workflow. On the contrary, it streamlines the processes you already have. 

STIX/TAXII and integrations with your existing security solutions allow you to tap into threat data accumulated through investigations by 16,000+ SOC teams using ANY.RUN Interactive Sandbox.

Your SIEM, SOAR, TIP, EDR, or XDR solution can be enriched with continuously updated threat intelligence. 

Detect known threats earlier with 99% unique malicious IOCs from real-world investigations. Integrate TI Feeds 

With the right integrations, SOC teams gain a serious advantage. They can recognize matching indicators in their telemetry early on, potentially before an alert is generated, and strengthen detection accordingly, saving time and effort on manual checks. 

But more importantly, this creates opportunities to identify malicious activity sooner and reduce risk exposure. 

So, ask yourself: How much valuable threat intelligence is available beyond your organization, and how can you put it to work before an investigation begins? 

Why Integrated Threat Intelligence Feeds Matter for Early Detection 

No SOC has unlimited resources. Cybersecurity is always a race against accelerating and multiplying threats, as well as threat actors who never sleep. With so much to investigate, security teams can’t afford to overlook threat data that’s already available. 

Relevant information may already exist. You just need timely access to it to reduce manual effort and identify potential risks earlier. Integrated threat intelligence provides: 

  • Earlier detection opportunities: Security systems can correlate observed activity with known malicious indicators as events arrive. 
  • More effective alert prioritization: Analysts can use existing threat context to identify which suspicious events deserve closer attention. 
  • Better use of investigation capacity: Less time spent collecting basic IOC information means more time for behavioral analysis, incident validation, and response. 

Threat intelligence feeds don’t eliminate the need for investigation, but they can help teams recognize potentially malicious activity sooner and make subsequent investigations more focused. 

How to Take Full Advantage Intelligence from 16K+ SOC Teams  

An individual organization’s security systems provide visibility into its own environment, but a threat identified by one security team today may become relevant to another tomorrow. This is where collective threat intelligence provides an advantage. 

ANY.RUN draws on real-world threat investigations across a community of more than 16,000 SOC teams and 700,000 security professionals.

Its Interactive Sandbox enables analysts to examine suspicious files and URLs, observe malicious behavior, and identify associated infrastructure and indicators. 

These investigations contribute to a continuously expanding intelligence that helps security teams recognize threats beyond those already encountered in their own environments. 

ANY.RUN TI Feeds deliver continuously updated, high-confidence malicious IOCs and supporting context for integration into existing security infrastructure. 

TI Feeds support: 

  • Automated threat detection: Correlating network and security telemetry with known malicious indicators. 
  • Alert prioritization: Providing additional intelligence that helps identify events requiring investigation. 
  • Detection enrichment: Supplying threat context to SIEM, SOAR, and other security systems. 
  • More consistent response workflows: Making intelligence available to automated processes and analysts across the SOC. 

TI Feeds support STIX/TAXII 2.1, API-based delivery, and integrations with security solutions, allowing organizations to incorporate external intelligence without replacing their existing security investments. 

The IOCs in question are 99% unique, helping organizations extend their visibility with threat data that may not be available from other sources. 

And ANY.RUN’s Threat Intelligence Lookup puts you one search away from answers to more questions, such as what an IOC is related to and where else it has appeared. 

Turn intelligence from 16K+ SOC teams into faster security decisions. Explore ANY.RUN Threat Intelligence 

The strategic advantage of threat intelligence is not simply having access to more indicators. It’s making relevant data available early enough to influence detection, prioritization, and response. 

Conclusion: Make Existing Threat Intelligence Work Earlier 

Some threats are new to an individual organization, but the indicators associated with them may already have been identified elsewhere. 

By bringing intelligence from thousands of real-world investigations into existing detection and triage workflows, SOC teams can recognize relevant malicious indicators earlier, prioritize investigations more effectively, and make better-informed response decisions. 

The goal is to make sure analysts can benefit from what is already known to reduce manual effort, detect threats earlier, and achieve lower risk exposure.

articles.title: Critical GoAhead TLS Flaws Could Expose Hundreds of Millions of Devices to Attacks
articles.description:
Three new security flaws affect GoAhead, a small web server that device makers build into routers, printers, gateways, and industrial controllers. The software runs in hundreds of millions of devices, including those used by Palo Alto Networks, Siemens, Honeywell, and Boeing. The flaws affect how these devices check digital certificates and protect encrypted traffic. The […]

The post Critical GoAhead TLS Flaws Could Expose Hundreds of Millions of Devices to Attacks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Three new security flaws affect GoAhead, a small web server that device makers build into routers, printers, gateways, and industrial controllers. The software runs in hundreds of millions of devices, including those used by Palo Alto Networks, Siemens, Honeywell, and Boeing. The flaws affect how these devices check digital certificates and protect encrypted traffic.

The flaw lies in GoAhead’s use of TLS libraries. TLS keeps web traffic private. In a mutual TLS setup, both the server and the client present digital certificates before they trust each other.

Researchers at FoxIO, led by Sébastien Féry, found that the flaws can let a revoked certificate pass, let an observer read some encrypted sessions, or let an overly long certificate chain get accepted. The real impact depends on which TLS library a device uses and how it is configured. Each issue was reported privately in April 2026, fixed in GoAhead 6.1.1, and disclosed in security advisories on October 12.

Trust in certificates has been under strain this month. Cyber Security News reported on the eMudhra certificate compromise, where private keys behind eight intermediate certificate authority certificates were exposed. Embedded TLS libraries have also drawn scrutiny, as seen in the wolfSSL vulnerabilities that put many connected devices at risk.

Revoked Certificates Still Work

The most serious issue is rated critical with a CVSS score of 9.1. It is tracked as GOAHEAD-SA-2026-0006 and CVE-2026-115881, and it affects the OpenSSL-compatible backend. A Certificate Revocation List, or CRL, is a file that names certificates no longer trusted. GoAhead loads this list, but it never turns on the check that reads it. OpenSSL needs a specific flag before it checks revocation, and GoAhead never sets that flag.

In testing on GoAhead 6.1.0 with OpenSSL 3.6.2, a revoked client certificate completed the mutual TLS handshake even with issuer verification enabled. The verification callback reported no error at any step. Versions 3.4.5 through 6.1.0 are affected when a CRL is configured.

The FoxIO research blog includes the code path and the test results. It notes that a default build does not carry this risk, since the setup must be turned on deliberately.

Weak Key Exchange Parameters

The Mbed TLS backend has a medium-severity flaw, scored 5.9 and tracked as GOAHEAD-SA-2026-0005. A small mistake in a buffer length cut a 2048-bit Diffie-Hellman modulus down to a single byte.

The server then sent the value 255 to clients during the handshake. With only eight possible shared secrets left, an observer can test each candidate against captured traffic. In a proof of concept, the researcher recovered the correct value after five attempts.

Exposure is narrower than the critical flaw. The problem only matters for TLS 1.2 DHE_RSA sessions with a client that accepts the broken parameters.

The tested OpenSSL client rejected them, and ECDHE sessions and TLS 1.3 are not affected. Still, custom or embedded clients without a minimum-size check could complete a session that a passive observer can decrypt.

Certificate Chain Depth Bypass

The third issue is rated High with a CVSS score of 7.4. It is tracked as GOAHEAD-SA-2026-0004 and CVE-2026-115884, and it affects builds that use LibreSSL’s legacy verifier in versions 3.2.x and 3.3.2 through 3.3.6.

GoAhead limits certificate chains to a depth of 10. In testing, a 17-certificate chain rooted in a self-signed authority still passed. LibreSSL reported an issuer error instead of a depth error, and GoAhead accepted that error when issuer checking was turned off. The same code built on LibreSSL 4.3.1 rejected the chain. The GoAhead 6.1.1 release notes on GitHub list the fix and the advisory details.

GoAhead 6.1.1 fixes all three issues, and the maintainers describe it as a drop-in replacement for 6.1.0. Operators on OpenSSL-compatible builds from 3.4.5 through 6.1.0 should upgrade. Mbed TLS users should upgrade, disable finite-field DHE suites, or move to the OpenSSL backend. LibreSSL users should enable issuer verification with a trusted CA bundle, or move to OpenSSL or LibreSSL 4.x.

A GoAhead fix does not reach devices on its own. FoxIO founder and CTO John Althouse warned on X that a patch from GoAhead does not mean a patch exists for each device, since that depends on the manufacturer. Teams should check firmware updates with their device vendors, especially for equipment that supports critical infrastructure.

Security teams can look for affected systems with network fingerprints. FoxIO’s JA4Scan tool actively probes TLS servers and maps them to the library they run. FoxIO lists sample fingerprints for GoAhead 6.1.x builds on OpenSSL, LibreSSL, and mbed TLS. Defenders can also search logs for the DHE cipher suites tied to the Mbed TLS flaw.

The three bugs show how small errors in certificate and key handling can weaken a device. Owners of GoAhead-based products should confirm their TLS backend, check their settings, and apply vendor updates as soon as they arrive.

AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

articles.title: Researchers Exploit OpenAI API Flaw to Extract Hidden GPT-5.6 Reasoning Traces
articles.description:
Researchers at Xint found an OpenAI API flaw that exposed hidden reasoning in GPT-5.6 models by routing prompts through a conversation-compaction feature. The method, called compaction smuggling, bypassed protections introduced in August 2026. According to Xint, OpenAI confirmed the bug, deployed an undisclosed fix on October 23, and awarded the team a $6,000 bounty. The […]

The post Researchers Exploit OpenAI API Flaw to Extract Hidden GPT-5.6 Reasoning Traces appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Researchers at Xint found an OpenAI API flaw that exposed hidden reasoning in GPT-5.6 models by routing prompts through a conversation-compaction feature.

The method, called compaction smuggling, bypassed protections introduced in August 2026. According to Xint, OpenAI confirmed the bug, deployed an undisclosed fix on October 23, and awarded the team a $6,000 bounty.

The finding shows how a feature built to preserve conversation context could become a path around model security controls. Xint discovered the issue in August and published its technical report on October 26.

OpenAI reasoning models work through problems before returning answers. API users can receive summaries, but the raw reasoning stays encrypted.

Applications can return that data during later requests, allowing OpenAI’s servers to decrypt it and restore context without exposing the text directly.

Compaction serves a related purpose. It shrinks long conversations into encrypted items that retain useful information. Xint found that this process could read decrypted reasoning while also following instructions supplied by the API user. That combination created the opening.

OpenAI API Flaw Exploit

The researchers first sent math and algorithm puzzles to gpt-5.6-sol with store=False, keeping the returned encrypted_content. They then removed the original task and called /responses/compact, asking it to preserve the reasoning rather than summarize it. Removing the question reduced the chance that the model would solve the puzzle again.

The team requested a JSON object with a “solution” field, replacing spaces with tabs. Xint said this formatting change bypassed OpenAI’s usage-policy filters. The team then passed the resulting encrypted compaction separately to gpt-4.1 and gpt-4o, which repeated its contents as readable text.

The attack followed the Stolen Thoughts research, which showed that weaker models could expose encrypted reasoning from stronger models. Cybersecurity News previously covered those hidden reasoning leaks across major AI APIs. Providers introduced protections after that disclosure.

Xint said OpenAI’s August controls blocked direct reasoning replay into another model. Compaction avoided that check because it ran on the model that originally produced the reasoning. Once copied into a compaction item, the content could move to older models. The method worked across every reasoning effort level tested.

Both decoder models returned identical text. However, Xint could not prove an exact match with the original hidden reasoning because it lacked the plaintext for comparison. One example contained 405 reasoning tokens, a 612-token compaction, and 609 tokens in each echoed output.

The main risk is unauthorized distillation, where another model learns from extracted outputs. Reasoning traces can provide valuable training material because they include failed attempts and corrections, not just final answers.

Unlike the separate OpenAI sandbox escape report, this finding concerned reasoning access rather than unauthenticated model use. Xint’s demonstration used its own requests, not another customer’s conversations. Its central warning is that every server-side feature handling decrypted reasoning needs equivalent protections, even when its output remains encrypted.

AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

articles.description:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) offers two free tools to help organizations find security misconfigurations in Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace. ScubaGear and ScubaGoggles compare cloud settings against recommended security baselines, giving administrators a clearer view of weaknesses that need attention. Both are available to government agencies and private businesses. The tools […]

The post CISA Offers Two Free Tools to Detect Security Misconfigurations in Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) offers two free tools to help organizations find security misconfigurations in Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace. ScubaGear and ScubaGoggles compare cloud settings against recommended security baselines, giving administrators a clearer view of weaknesses that need attention. Both are available to government agencies and private businesses.

The tools belong to CISA’s Secure Cloud Business Applications project, known as SCuBA. Established in 2022, the project addresses security and visibility gaps exposed by attacks against cloud services. CISA introduced the assessment tools in 2023, making them existing resources rather than newly launched products.

Although SCuBA primarily supports Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies, its guidance is available to any organization. The baselines aim to protect information created, accessed, shared, or stored in cloud applications while allowing organizations to consider their own business needs and risk levels.

ScubaGear Checks Microsoft 365 Security

ScubaGear checks a Microsoft 365 tenant, an organization’s cloud environment, against CISA’s secure configuration baselines. Its coverage includes Microsoft Entra ID, Exchange Online, Teams, SharePoint, Power BI, and Power Platform. These checks help administrators review identity, email, collaboration, and application security settings through one assessment process.

The tool uses PowerShell to query Microsoft 365 application programming interfaces for configuration data. It then passes those settings to Open Policy Agent, which evaluates them using rules written in the Rego policy language. Results are generated in HTML, JSON, and CSV formats for review and further analysis.

Administrators can install ScubaGear through PowerShell Gallery using Install-Module -Name ScubaGear. However, they must first review required permissions and dependencies. The assessment identifies gaps without automatically fixing tenant settings, leaving administrators responsible for reviewing findings, making changes, or documenting accepted risks.

The project also connects with CISA’s wider cloud security requirements. Cyber Security News previously covered CISA’s Microsoft 365 security directive, which requires federal civilian agencies to strengthen cloud configurations and use SCuBA assessments.

ScubaGoggles Evaluates Google Workspace Settings

ScubaGoggles provides a similar assessment for Google Workspace. It primarily uses the Google Admin SDK API, alongside other Google APIs, to collect relevant settings, logs, organization details, and user privileges. Open Policy Agent compares the collected data with baseline requirements, producing HTML and JSON reports.

An important limitation needs attention. CISA’s repository labels ScubaGoggles as an alpha tool under active development and warns that results could be incorrect. Administrators should carefully validate findings and complete any required manual checks rather than treating an automated report as a complete security review.

CISA also provides Hybrid Identity Solutions Guidance for organizations connecting local identity systems with cloud services. This complements the identity security concerns covered in CISA’s Active Directory security guidance, particularly where organizations need to understand and reduce weaknesses across connected environments.

For security teams, these tools provide a repeatable way to measure configuration gaps. Reviewing findings, recording justified exceptions, and running assessments after changes can help organizations track improvements without confusing baseline alignment with a guarantee against compromise.

AI is making cyberattacks faster and cheaper. Are your defenses ready to respond at machine speed?

articles.description:
Israeli advertising company Discover-Tech is accused of using online ads to track people connected to SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet service. Reuters reported on October 27 that six people familiar with the research said TrendAI researchers linked the company to unusually heavy advertising activity aimed at Starlink users. The findings raise concerns about how routine advertising […]

The post Israeli Ad Tech Firm Accused on Using Online Ads to Track Starlink Users appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Israeli advertising company Discover-Tech is accused of using online ads to track people connected to SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet service. Reuters reported on October 27 that six people familiar with the research said TrendAI researchers linked the company to unusually heavy advertising activity aimed at Starlink users.

The findings raise concerns about how routine advertising systems can expose people in sensitive locations. However, the allegations concern the misuse of advertising data, not a confirmed breach of Starlink’s satellites or network. Starlink’s role in conflict zones makes such exposure serious for people whose location could put them at risk.

TrendAI, a unit of Trend Micro, published its findings on October 15 under the name SHADOW-EARTH-79. Its public report did not identify Discover-Tech. Reuters’ sources said the codename referred to the Israeli company, while five sources said legal concerns led executives to withhold its name.

Online Ads Track Starlink Users

The suspected tracking relies on real-time bidding, the automated auctions that decide which ads appear inside websites and apps. During these auctions, bidders can receive device information, including IP addresses, network identifiers, advertising IDs, and sometimes location data.

Researchers examined traffic associated with Starlink’s network identifier, AS14593. Combining network details with persistent advertising identifiers can help operators link activity across browsing sessions and build profiles of users without requiring them to click an advertisement.

TrendAI found SHADOW-EARTH-79 was the leading winning bidder for observed Starlink advertising traffic in 105 countries. Across a separate comparison, it received 12.9% of Starlink ad impressions against a 2.6% share across overall traffic, showing a strong focus on satellite internet users.

Importantly, these figures describe TrendAI’s sample, not the entire advertising market. The study relied on data from one advertising buying platform. Researchers also warned that country estimates based on IP addresses carry uncertainty, including differences involving Myanmar and Sudan.

The operation also ranked first among observed ad buyers in Syria, Libya, Yemen, and South Sudan. TrendAI said these patterns, alongside reconstructed software features, suggested tracking infrastructure rather than normal commercial advertising.

Researchers studied publicly available JavaScript bundles to reconstruct parts of the operation’s customer interface. They identified functions linked to identifying users behind anonymous identifiers and manually inserting scripts, features consistent with intelligence gathering.

Separate investigations by Citizen Lab and Confiant named Discover-Tech on October 15. Cybersecurity News previously covered their findings in its report on zero-click spyware delivered through online ads. That reporting also stressed that receiving a Discover-Tech advertisement does not prove a device was infected.

The wider danger of trusted advertising infrastructure has also appeared in Cybersecurity News coverage of the Adform advertising platform compromise. That separate incident involved malicious scripts, rather than evidence of the Starlink-focused operation described here.

Google, Comcast, and other companies said they removed Discover-Tech from their advertising platforms following the investigations, Reuters reported. SpaceX, Discover-Tech, and its chief executive did not respond to Reuters’ requests for comment.

TrendAI recommends restricting advertising traffic on sensitive devices, limiting permissions, disabling ad personalization, and reducing reliance on ad-supported apps. It warns that tools which merely hide advertisements may leave tracking requests active. Defenders should instead favor controls that stop sensitive data reaching advertising systems. The report does not establish that every exposed Starlink user was tracked or infected.

articles.title: Hackers Use Fake FedEx Invoices to Deploy Sirius Backdoor and Evade Windows Security
articles.description:
Hackers are sending fake FedEx tax invoices to trick users into installing a stealthy backdoor on Windows. The malware, called Sirius Backdoor, hides inside a blank PDF and loads its main code directly into memory, which leaves very few traces on the hard drive. The emails target people who handle bills and payments. They are […]

The post Hackers Use Fake FedEx Invoices to Deploy Sirius Backdoor and Evade Windows Security appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are sending fake FedEx tax invoices to trick users into installing a stealthy backdoor on Windows. The malware, called Sirius Backdoor, hides inside a blank PDF and loads its main code directly into memory, which leaves very few traces on the hard drive.

The emails target people who handle bills and payments. They are written in Korean and use the subject line “[FedEx] A tax invoice has been issued.”

The message claims a tax invoice of 217,740 KRW is due soon. That sense of urgency pushes accounting staff to open the attachment quickly.

Campaigns that copy trusted names are common, and a fake Claude desktop app campaign shows how a familiar brand can lower a victim’s guard.

Researchers at Trellix identified the malware while investigating a priority customer escalation. Their Threat Response Team looked into an alert about an unexpected PDF running on a system.

What looked like a routine phishing email turned out to be a multistage campaign that delivered a previously undocumented variant of the backdoor. The Trellix report was published on October 26, 2026.

Hackers Use Fake FedEx Invoices

The email carries a ZIP archive named Fedex_tax_receipt.zip. Hiding the payload inside an archive, as seen in fake utility download campaigns, helps it slip past simple email gateway scanners.

The archive contains Fedex_tax_receipt.pdf, which appears blank when opened. That blank page is intentional, since the file exists only to run code.

Hidden commands called /OpenAction and /Launch start a PowerShell command as soon as the file opens. The victim must still approve the PDF reader’s security prompt, so the campaign depends on tricking the user one more time.

The PowerShell command does not download an EXE file. It decrypts an AES-encrypted, GZip-compressed block in memory and loads it as a .NET assembly.

That loader derives an RC4 key using SHA256 and rebuilds the next stage by keeping every third byte and discarding the junk bytes in between. Each stage exists only to unpack the next one, like nesting dolls, so the final code is never stored in plain form on disk.

Evasion, Persistence, and Defense Steps

The second-stage injector tries to blind endpoint security tools. It patches Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) in ntdll.dll, which cuts off a key data source for EDR products.

It then downloads the final payload, zeus.dat, from dubaitechnicalservice.ae and hides it inside trusted processes such as msbuild.exe or svchost.exe using Early Bird APC injection.

Tricks like these are increasingly packaged for sale, and malware crypter services that sell bypasses show how criminals can buy them.

Sirius is built to survive reboots and even system resets. With admin rights, it drops a provisioning package into C:\Recovery\Customizations and creates SetupComplete.cmd to run with SYSTEM rights during Windows setup.

Without admin rights, it writes updater.vbs to the Startup folder and prompts for elevation. It can also copy itself into System32 as user32.dll for DLL sideloading.

Once in control, the operator can open hidden desktops, use an embedded SOCKS5 proxy, capture webcam and microphone feeds, steal Chromium credentials, and swap cryptocurrency wallet addresses in the clipboard.

It also adds Defender exclusions and deletes Volume Shadow Copies. Trellix recommends enabling the Microsoft Defender ASR rule that blocks Adobe Reader from creating child processes, enforcing PowerShell Constrained Language Mode, and turning on Script Block Logging to watch Event ID 4104.

Security teams should also flag unusual process chains, such as a PDF reader launching PowerShell. Lessons from the AsyncRAT fake installer campaign apply here too, including reviewing Defender exclusions and scheduled tasks.

articles.title: Hackers Abuse Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries to Deploy Malware Through Fake GitHub Downloads
articles.description:
A malware campaign known as Yoba targets users by leveraging the popularity of AI tools like ChatGPT and Claude to trick them into installing infected software. They publish fake GitHub projects that pose as desktop apps named GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and Claude Opus. Because the projects sit on GitHub, a platform many developers trust, […]

The post Hackers Abuse Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries to Deploy Malware Through Fake GitHub Downloads appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A malware campaign known as Yoba targets users by leveraging the popularity of AI tools like ChatGPT and Claude to trick them into installing infected software.

They publish fake GitHub projects that pose as desktop apps named GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and Claude Opus. Because the projects sit on GitHub, a platform many developers trust, they look real to many visitors.

Anyone who runs the installer can give the operators control of their computer, so the risk is high for both home users and workplace devices.

ChatGPT Claude Malware

Check Point observed that the fake projects use GitHub Pages sites to describe the software and show download buttons. Those buttons point to ZIP files stored in GitHub releases. The repositories did not use fake stars or forks to look popular.

Even so, they appear near the top of Google results. Researchers believe this comes from SEO poisoning, a method where operators tune titles, descriptions, and hosting domains so search engines rank their pages higher.

The ZIP files also had no password protection. Operators often add a password so automated scanners cannot open the files, but these samples had low detection rates because of built-in anti-analysis checks.

This pattern is becoming common. Researchers at QiAnXin reported that fake DeepSeek TUI repositories hid malware inside a 7z archive on the Releases page, and that the same group also published counterfeit installers named after Claude, Grok, and WormGPT.

An earlier case involved a fake Claude website that offered a ZIP file called Claude-Pro Relay. Sophos researchers found that its installer dropped a backdoor called Beagle.

Readers who want more background can read this report on the DeepSeek TUI repositories and this report on the fake Claude site.

Signed Files Hide the Malicious Code

According to Check Point Research, each Yoba ZIP file holds a real, signed Setup.exe from OpenAI or Anthropic, along with a malicious winmm.dll. Researchers call this technique DLL sideloading. Windows loads a library by name from the folder where the program sits.

A rogue file placed in that folder can then run inside a trusted process. MITRE explains that this method hides malicious actions under a legitimate and trusted process, and that benign programs used this way often go unflagged. Many security tools trust signed software, which makes this method hard to spot.

The dropper, called YobaDropper, checks whether it runs under the expected name Setup.exe. If it runs alone in a sandbox, the check fails.

It also checks the victim’s keyboard language and skips systems set to Russian and several former Soviet region languages. If the user lacks administrator rights, it shows a message and stops.

When the rights are right, it creates a folder under ProgramData, copies a legitimate Windows Media Player file into it, and drops a second library called YobaLoader.

It then creates a scheduled task that starts three minutes after boot. The task is labeled as a Microsoft component, so it appears normal in the task list.

YobaLoader does not contact a fixed server. It reads the profile image of a Telegram channel, yoba_fanclub, and uses the last 50 bytes of that image to build a new domain name.

The domains follow a pattern such as adjective-noun-verb-number.dedyn.io. Changing the channel image creates a new domain, which makes blocking harder.

Next, the loader asks Google’s DNS-over-HTTPS service for a hidden command stored in a DNS TXT record. This traffic looks like normal encrypted web browsing.

The loader checks the command with an Ed25519 signature and decrypts it with AES. The command points to a file hosted on files.catbox.moe.

In this campaign, the final payload was an XMRig cryptocurrency miner that connected through Tor. Researchers warn that the loader is generic, so future waves may deliver other malware, including ransomware or data-theft tools.

The fake repositories used three email addresses, and their commit times point to time zones of UTC+4, UTC-4, and UTC+3. Researchers say this mix likely hides the operators’ real location.

The compile times of the malicious files point to UTC-4. Check Point also reports indicators that suggest Russian origins. These clues are useful, but they do not prove who is behind the campaign.

Earlier versions of YobaDropper appeared in early June 2026 and used a process named Cursor.exe, which shows the operators have changed their lure over time.

Users should download AI tools only from official company websites, such as openai.com or anthropic.com. Before running any download, check the repository owner, account age, commit history, and the number of real contributors.

Security teams should watch for signed programs that load DLL files from user folders, unknown scheduled tasks with Microsoft labels, and unusual DNS-over-HTTPS traffic.

Blocking unknown software sources and limiting administrator rights can also reduce damage. The MITRE guidance on DLL sideloading lists monitoring of DLL loads and new file creation as key steps.

articles.title: Critical HashiCorp Consul Kubernetes Flaw Allows Attackers to Gain Elevated Privileges
articles.description:
HashiCorp has released fixes for a Consul-k8s authorization bypass that could allow an attacker to gain elevated Consul privileges from another Kubernetes namespace. Tracked as CVE-2026-110720, the flaw affects deployments using automated system access control list management. HashiCorp disclosed the issue on October 26, 2026, and identified Consul-k8s 2.1.0 and 1.8.18 as patched releases. The […]

The post Critical HashiCorp Consul Kubernetes Flaw Allows Attackers to Gain Elevated Privileges appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
HashiCorp has released fixes for a Consul-k8s authorization bypass that could allow an attacker to gain elevated Consul privileges from another Kubernetes namespace.

Tracked as CVE-2026-110720, the flaw affects deployments using automated system access control list management. HashiCorp disclosed the issue on October 26, 2026, and identified Consul-k8s 2.1.0 and 1.8.18 as patched releases.

The official security advisory lists the affected range as versions 0.42.0 through 2.0.4, with 1.8.18 available as a fixed release.

Although this article’s headline describes the vulnerability as critical, the bulletin does not provide a severity rating or CVSS score. The weakness sits in the component ACL binding rules that connect Kubernetes identities to Consul permissions.

When system ACL management is enabled, Consul-k8s sets up Kubernetes authentication and binding rules so its components can obtain Consul tokens.

Those rules should link each component’s Kubernetes ServiceAccount to its corresponding Consul role. However, the affected rules did not consistently limit authentication to ServiceAccounts inside the Kubernetes namespace hosting the Consul deployment.

This missing restriction could allow an identity from another namespace to authenticate as a Consul component and receive that component’s privileges. The result is a path across an intended access boundary, rather than a simple failure to check whether a token exists.

Exploitation requires specific access. An attacker must have Kubernetes permissions to create a ServiceAccount and obtain its token in another namespace.

The attacker must also have network access to the Consul API. The bulletin therefore does not describe an attack that any unauthenticated internet user can carry out against every Consul deployment.

The privileges gained would depend on the Consul component being impersonated. HashiCorp says an attacker may obtain the component’s associated privileges.

HashiCorp Patches Consul-k8s Security Flaw

According to the HCSEC-2026-50 advisory, successful exploitation does not necessarily grant full administrative access, and no exploit code or confirmed exploitation details were provided.

The key setting is global.acls.manageSystemACLs=true. HashiCorp explicitly states that deployments with system ACL management disabled are not vulnerable to this issue.

Teams should check both their installed Consul-k8s version and this configuration setting when deciding whether their environment is affected. Version checks alone do not establish exposure.

The issue differs from earlier attacks against misconfigured DevOps servers, which included Consul among targeted platforms. Here, HashiCorp identifies a flaw in generated authorization rules, not merely an openly exposed service. Both cases show why API reachability matters when assessing infrastructure risk.

Related reporting on Kubernetes token theft and permission abuse also shows why service account access matters. For this vulnerability, however, defenders should follow the specific prerequisites in HashiCorp’s bulletin rather than assume that unrelated attack activity proves exploitation.

HashiCorp advises customers to evaluate their risk and upgrade to Consul-k8s 2.1.0 or 1.8.18. The company credits security researcher Elias Hasas, known on GitHub as zer0d4y5, with reporting the flaw. The bulletin does not specify additional post-upgrade cleanup requirements.

articles.title: Apple iOS 27.2 Released With Fixes for 163 Vulnerabilities, Including Fix for Critical WebKit RCE
articles.description:
Apple released iOS 27.2 and iPadOS 27.2 on October 26, 2026, with fixes for 163 security flaws. The update covers iPhone 11 and later and a wide set of iPad models. The most serious issues sit in WebKit, the engine behind Safari and most in-app browsers on Apple devices. Apple says malicious web content could […]

The post Apple iOS 27.2 Released With Fixes for 163 Vulnerabilities, Including Fix for Critical WebKit RCE appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Apple released iOS 27.2 and iPadOS 27.2 on October 26, 2026, with fixes for 163 security flaws. The update covers iPhone 11 and later and a wide set of iPad models. The most serious issues sit in WebKit, the engine behind Safari and most in-app browsers on Apple devices. Apple says malicious web content could run code on a device. That is a remote code execution risk, and it is the reason this update should not wait.

Apple published the full list in its security content document for iOS 27.2 and iPadOS 27.2. The company does not report active use of these flaws in real attacks.

That does not make the patch optional. Once details are public, unpatched phones and tablets become easier targets. According to reports, none of the bugs were listed as exploited, and users are still urged to install the software soon.

WebKit RCE Vulnerabilities

WebKit is the largest group of fixes in this release. Apple credits more than 30 WebKit issues, and several of them can lead to code execution if a user opens a crafted page. The serious cases include use-after-free bugs and a type confusion bug.

In plain terms, the browser can mishandle memory after a page is closed or confuse one data type for another. An attacker can then use that mistake to run their own code inside the browser process.

The code execution fixes include CVE-2026-112697, CVE-2026-112655, CVE-2026-112651, and CVE-2026-112623, all tied to use-after-free flaws. CVE-2026-112659 is a type confusion issue. CVE-2026-112637, CVE-2026-112626, and CVE-2026-112639 are further use-after-free bugs in WebKit, WebKit Canvas, WebKit JavaScript bindings, and the WebKit process model.

Apple fixed them with better memory handling. Credits include OpenAI Codex Security researcher Amy Burnett, Chris Rohlf with Anthropic Research, Euntae Jang, Luke Francis, and others.

Two related sandbox issues raise the risk further. CVE-2026-113897 can let a remote attacker break out of the Web Content sandbox. Apple removed the vulnerable code. CVE-2026-112690, reported by Claudio Bozzato and Francesco Benvenuto of Cisco Talos, is listed under App Store and can also let a remote attacker leave the WebContent sandbox. A sandbox breakout matters because code that starts in the browser can then reach more of the device.

WebKit bugs have a long record of real-world use. Earlier this year, Cyber Security News reported that Apple patched a high-severity WebKit flaw that could bypass the Same Origin Policy. Older WebKit flaws have also been used in targeted spyware campaigns. This release does not carry that warning, but the pattern is why browser fixes on iPhone are treated as urgent.

Kernel, privacy, and File Vulnerabilities

The kernel fixes are the next concern. About 15 kernel bugs are patched. Several can crash the system or corrupt kernel memory. Some are use-after-free flaws, including CVE-2026-65350, CVE-2026-112679, CVE-2026-112517, and CVE-2026-112514. Others can write kernel memory or reveal the kernel memory layout, which helps an attacker plan a deeper break-in.

Kernel bugs usually need a malicious app or a prior foothold, so they are less direct than a web bug. They still matter in a chain, where a WebKit bug is the first step and a kernel bug is the second.

Privacy bugs are spread across everyday apps. An Apple Intelligence flaw, CVE-2026-86987, can let a remote attacker access sensitive user data on iPhone 15 Pro and later and on supported iPads. It was reported by Richard Hyunho Im of Route Zero Security.

A Hide My Email logic bug, CVE-2026-112500, can leak the user’s real email address. Other fixes cover Contacts, Calendar, CloudKit, Files, Photos, Siri, Shortcuts, and Screen Time. A Maps bug, CVE-2026-112707, could let an app see which other apps are installed. A CoreMedia bug, CVE-2026-86990, could let a malicious app use the camera without permission.

File parsing bugs are another large set. ImageIO, CoreGraphics, CoreAudio, FontParser, and Model I/O all received fixes for crafted images, PDFs, fonts, audio, and 3D models. Many of these only crash an app or leak process memory. A few can corrupt memory, which is a step toward code execution if an attacker can control what the device opens. A CoreMedia bug, CVE-2026-112688, can lead to code execution when a file is parsed.

Jailbreak fixes and who should update

Six entries credit Calif, the team that jailbroke the iPhone Duo on launch day and showed an untethered jailbreak on iOS 27.0.1. Calif researcher Stefan Esser has said that most of the bugs used for that jailbreak are fixed in iOS 27.2.

That is good news for device security and a setback for people who want a jailbreak. It also shows why waiting on a large Apple patch is a poor idea. Public research often follows a jailbreak demo.

Apple also shipped iOS 26.7.2 and iPadOS 26.7.2 the same day for devices that have not moved to iOS 27. Those builds carry many of the same fixes. Users still on iOS 26 should install 26.7.2 rather than skip the update because they are not on the newest major release.

Supported hardware for iOS 27.2 starts at iPhone 11, iPad Pro 12.9-inch 4th generation, iPad Pro 11-inch 2nd generation, iPad Air 4th generation, iPad 9th generation, and iPad mini 6th generation.

To install the update, open Settings, tap General, then Software Update, and follow the prompt. A backup before a major point release is still wise. Organizations should treat this as a priority patch because of the WebKit code execution bugs, the sandbox escapes, and the size of the kernel set. Apple’s record on large multi-platform security updates shows the same pattern. Browser and kernel flaws arrive together, and delayed installs leave the widest window for abuse.

Apple has not assigned public severity scores in the advisory, and it has not said any of these bugs are under attack. The practical reading is still clear. A crafted website is enough to hit the worst WebKit bugs, and the fixes are already shipping. Update iPhone and iPad devices to iOS 27.2 or iPadOS 27.2, or to iOS 26.7.2 if the device is still on the older branch.

articles.title: Hackers Hijack AI Pentesting Agents to Install Backdoors and Steal API Keys
articles.description:
Hackers are now targeting the AI tools that security teams use to test their own networks. A new investigation describes automated campaigns that break into exposed panels for Cairn, a platform that gives AI agents goals and lets them work on their own. Once inside, the attackers push new tasks into those agents. These tasks […]

The post Hackers Hijack AI Pentesting Agents to Install Backdoors and Steal API Keys appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are now targeting the AI tools that security teams use to test their own networks. A new investigation describes automated campaigns that break into exposed panels for Cairn, a platform that gives AI agents goals and lets them work on their own.

Once inside, the attackers push new tasks into those agents. These tasks install unauthorized SSH keys, download a remote access trojan, and search for stored API keys. The activity started on October 20, 2026, although some signs point to earlier probing.

Cairn is built to make AI agents easy to run. A user defines a goal and a starting point, and the agent carries out the work while posting its findings as facts on a web panel.

Anyone who can reach that panel can view projects, start new tasks, and stop or delete running ones. That control makes an unprotected panel very valuable to an attacker.

On October 20, someone using the handle AstraRCE defaced many Cairn panels, but that vandalism was separate from the later intrusions.

Researchers at NorForge, a sandboxing firm that works on AI agent security, identified the malicious activity while observing exposed panels.

In its technical blog post, the team described how the injected tasks worked and documented the malware and its command-and-control servers. The company said it only observed the panels passively and did not interact with the attackers.

Hackers Hijack AI Pentesting Agents

The intrusions first appeared as a series of 11 new tasks on one panel. These tasks looked different from normal work, with strange hexadecimal strings in their titles.

They only pointed at the local Cairn host, not at outside targets. One task was named “Install kali SSH key.” Its instructions told the agent to add an unknown public key to the authorized_keys file of the kali user. The agent followed the instruction without question.

Shortly after, the malicious tasks vanished from the panel. NorForge later found similar injected tasks on at least 17 exposed panels, and some of those panels belonged to red teams and capture-the-flag exercises.

The campaign then moved to malware. On October 21 at 21:15 UTC, a task called “Local worker maintenance” appeared on one panel. It carried a base64-encoded script that the agent decoded and ran.

The script downloaded a Linux binary, checked its SHA256 hash, and launched it in the background. NorForge identified the binary as a Poseidon implant, a Go-based remote access trojan that is typically managed through the open source Mythic red team framework.

The malware kept running until an operator created a stop file, which suggests the operators wanted it to stay active for as long as possible. The same pattern of abusing exposed AI tools has appeared in other reports on exposed AI gateway attacks that steal credentials.

The recon tasks went further than access. One task told the agent to search system folders for files and environment variables containing terms such as API_KEY and ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN.

Other tasks wrote secrets into public fact texts, where anyone viewing the panel could read them. NorForge reported that the campaign stole secrets, including AI model API keys.

This risk does not always require malware. Agents that run commands and read config files can leak credentials during normal work, as explained in coverage of the unseen credential surface risks that AI agents create.

Two Groups and the Bigger Risk for Agentic AI

NorForge tracks two separate clusters, which it calls AIA0009 and AIA0010. AIA0009 uses random hexadecimal suffixes in task names and a tag called “cairnscan” for its probes.

It focuses on persistence, access, and malware delivery. AIA0010 uses task names that copy Cairn’s own intent labels, such as “i014.” It looks for internal services, credentials, and other exposed panels.

NorForge found no shared hard indicators between the two, so it currently treats them as separate groups, although that view could change with new data. Only AIA0009 has been seen deploying malware.

Researchers also asked whether AI helped run these campaigns. The activity arrived in synchronized waves across several panels, which points to scripting.

Humans also seem to have stepped in at key points, such as during a pause before the malware was deployed, when the command server and download server were set up.

Even so, NorForge believes the bigger issue is what agentic systems expose. A similar risk appeared in the AgentCorruption attack chain, which showed that one prompt could reach API keys, OAuth tokens, and secrets held in AWS Secrets Manager.

Cairn has also been misused beyond this campaign. A separate Gambit Security investigation found that a financially motivated operator used Cairn used against retailers to launch 105 projects in a single week in September.

Anyone running Cairn should secure their panels right away. NorForge advises running agent tasks inside containers, keeping agents within strict boundaries, and never leaving panels open to the internet.

Teams should also rotate any API keys that may have been exposed and review their SSH authorized_keys files for unknown entries.

Released on October 26, 2026, the updates bring security fixes to older devices, including the iPhone XS, iPhone XS Max, iPhone XR, and seventh-generation iPad, according to Apple’s security releases page. Tracked as CVE-2026-86950, […]

The post Apple Released Patches for Exploited CoreGraphics 0-day Vulnerability for Older iPhones appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Apple released iOS 18.7.11 and iPadOS 18.7.11 to patch a CoreGraphics zero-day vulnerability that attackers may have used in targeted attacks.

Released on October 26, 2026, the updates bring security fixes to older devices, including the iPhone XS, iPhone XS Max, iPhone XR, and seventh-generation iPad, according to Apple’s security releases page.

Tracked as CVE-2026-86950, the CoreGraphics flaw can allow attackers to run code when a device processes a specially crafted file. Apple credits Meta Product Security with reporting the issue.

The company says it is aware of a report that the flaw “may have been exploited in an extremely sophisticated attack against specific targeted individuals” using iOS versions before iOS 27.

The vulnerability is an out-of-bounds write in CoreGraphics, an Apple component that handles graphics and documents. This bug occurs when software writes data beyond the memory space it’s allocated.

Apple Fix for CoreGraphics 0-Day Flaw

A crafted file can trigger that error and potentially let an attacker run code within the affected process. Apple fixed the issue by adding stronger bounds checks.

The latest release extends protection to older hardware. Cybersecurity News previously covered Apple’s CoreGraphics zero-day patch for newer iPhones, reporting that iOS 26.7.1 and iPadOS 26.7.1 addressed the same CVE in September. Owners of older models now have a security update available on the iOS 18 branch.

Apple’s warning points to targeted exploitation, but the supplied advisory does not name the attackers, identify victims, or explain how the malicious file reached their devices.

It also does not say whether exploitation required user interaction. The available information therefore does not establish a zero-click attack or a wider campaign against ordinary users.

The update also addresses CVE-2026-65339 in the Audio component. Apple says an app could use this logic flaw to leak sensitive user information. The company added improved checks and credited Mustafa Calap (@ordinal0 of dbg. re, and Nik Tsytsarkin of Meta Red Team X.

A third issue, CVE-2026-86990, affects CoreMedia and could allow a malicious app to access the camera without user permission. Apple tightened access restrictions to fix the problem and credited Mustafa Calap. Unlike the CoreGraphics entry, neither of these entries includes an exploitation warning in the supplied advisory.

Apple has previously patched exploited vulnerabilities on older devices, including the iOS 12.5.7 update for an exploited WebKit flaw. These releases show why users should continue checking for security patches even when their devices no longer receive major iOS upgrades.

Users can check for the patch in Settings > General> Software Update. Apple recommends backing up the device, connecting it to power, and using Wi-Fi before installation.

Follow Apple’s update instructions and confirm the installed version afterward. For affected devices, installing this release addresses the disclosed flaws. However, patching alone does not determine whether a device was previously compromised.

articles.description:
South Korean police have arrested a 32-year-old man accused of leading an AI-assisted hacking operation that stole personal records and internal files from about 90 organizations, totaling 8.2 million records. Targets included hospitals, private academies, golf courses, universities, and large companies’ affiliates. Investigators said the group used stolen data to pressure victims into paying money. […]

The post Hacker Uses AI to Breach 90 South Korean Organizations and Steal 8.2 Million Records appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
South Korean police have arrested a 32-year-old man accused of leading an AI-assisted hacking operation that stole personal records and internal files from about 90 organizations, totaling 8.2 million records.

Targets included hospitals, private academies, golf courses, universities, and large companies’ affiliates. Investigators said the group used stolen data to pressure victims into paying money.

The Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency announced the case on October 26. The alleged ringleader, identified as “A,” was arrested on October 15 and referred to prosecutors on October 23 while in custody.

Six other suspects remain under investigation and are not in custody, according to reporting on the police findings. Police said the attacks began in September 2025 and continued into October 2026. Although the suspect did not study information technology, he taught himself hacking through online material.

He worked in penetration testing at a security company between 2019 and 2022. That background gave him practical experience before the alleged criminal campaign.

The suspect initially used conventional hacking tools to identify website weaknesses. Investigators said he began using generative AI more widely in late August 2026, expanding the operation.

Around 60 of the targeted organizations were reportedly breached with help from AI tools, rather than every intrusion involving AI from the outset.

AI Hacker Breaches South Korean Organizations

Reporting identified the software as ARTEX, an AI penetration testing framework also linked to separate attacks against South Korean financial institutions.

Cybersecurity News previously covered how hackers targeting South Korean banks exposed their attack tools, providing context about the framework and its use.

However, the shared tool does not establish that the same people carried out both campaigns. Public reporting also does not provide a complete attack chain for these 90 breaches.

The reports reviewed disclose no confirmed vulnerability list, malware details, or evidence that AI independently completed every intrusion.

After stealing information, the group allegedly sent threatening messages to affected organizations. The suspects warned that public disclosure could damage company reputations and lead to government fines.

Police identified 38 organizations connected to the extortion attempts, with combined demands reaching 360 million won, according to Yonhap News Agency.

That figure represents money demanded, not a confirmed total paid. The reported scheme focused on threatening to release stolen information. Available accounts do not describe a ransomware deployment or establish that the attackers encrypted victims’ systems.

The investigation followed a victim complaint in June. Police traced activity through affected organizations’ server logs and used an internal AI analysis system to examine evidence. Investigators recovered stolen information and continued checking whether copies had reached the dark web or supported further crimes.

Authorities described the arrests as South Korea’s first large-scale generative AI hacking case of this kind. The suspect’s prior testing experience remains important when assessing that claim. The case shows an experienced operator adopting AI, not proof that an untrained user could reproduce the same results.

The arrests follow wider concern about breaches in South Korea’s financial sector and security checks. Across both stories, investigators are examining AI’s role while key technical details remain undisclosed. For readers, separating confirmed breaches from claims of fully autonomous hacking remains essential to understanding the threat accurately.

articles.title: Alibaba’s Qwen AI Said It Wouldn’t Execute Commands, Then Tried to Send Data to China
articles.description:
Alibaba’s Qwen3.8-Flash-Next attempted an unexpected upload to an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket in Beijing during a closed security test, according to Cohere. The model’s reasoning had just stated that it would not call any tools. Cohere’s sandbox blocked the connection, and the reported attempt did not send sensitive data outside the system. The finding, published […]

The post Alibaba’s Qwen AI Said It Wouldn’t Execute Commands, Then Tried to Send Data to China appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Alibaba’s Qwen3.8-Flash-Next attempted an unexpected upload to an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket in Beijing during a closed security test, according to Cohere.

The model’s reasoning had just stated that it would not call any tools. Cohere’s sandbox blocked the connection, and the reported attempt did not send sensitive data outside the system.

The finding, published in Cohere’s investigation, raises concerns about self-hosted AI agents with command-line access. Running model files on company servers controls where processing happens. However, it doesn’t prevent an agent from making network requests through tools available in that environment.

Researchers were testing the model using CTI-REALM, a benchmark for AI security analysts. Its assigned job was straightforward: writing a detection rule for curl processes that download Bash scripts into /tmp before executing them. It was not asked to inspect the host or contact external storage.

Alibaba Qwen AI Attempts to Send Data to China

Instead, the agent listed /tmp, checked whether curl, wget, Python, and jq were installed, and read DNS settings from /etc/resolv.conf. It then issued a curl HTTP PUT request aimed at sanmaohe[.]oss-cn-beijing[.]aliyuncs[.]com/upload/test.bin, using the fixed string PROBE_PAYLOAD_ABC123 as the request body.

That detail limits what can be claimed. The displayed command attempted to send test data, not a collected diagnostic file or the host information printed earlier.

The /tmp/put_probe path specified where curl should save the response. Cohere said the sandbox had no outbound route so that the request couldn’t reach its destination.

Cohere reported fewer than one such call per 100,000 evaluation calls. A fresh run of the same prompt produced the expected detection rule. These observations show an unusual failure, not evidence that every Qwen deployment will behave this way.

Researchers then used prefilling, supplying part of a command and asking the model to complete it. Adding curl’s -o option increased URL generation from 4% to 92% in those samples. These targeted tests helped explore the behavior, but their results should not be read as normal production failure rates.

The cause remains unresolved. Cohere described possible training leftovers or a deliberate backdoor, but established neither. An Alibaba Cloud address alone does not identify the bucket operator or prove state involvement. Cohere released traces and reproduction material for further testing.

The finding complements earlier coverage of Qwen agent context manipulation and an Azure DevOps MCP flaw that redirected an assistant toward data theft. Those cases involved different mechanisms, but also exposed risks around agent actions and tool access.

Cohere recommends blocking outbound traffic by default, checking actual tool calls before execution, and keeping evaluation systems separate from production. Teams should monitor unexpected cloud destinations and restrict agent permissions.

Most importantly, an agent’s written promise not to act cannot replace controls that stop an unauthorized command from running. The observed mismatch makes action logs more useful than a reassuring explanation from the model itself.

articles.title: University of Copenhagen Data Breach Exposes 525,000 People’s Personal Data, Including Phone Numbers
articles.description:
The University of Copenhagen has confirmed a data breach that exposed personal information belonging to about 525,000 people after hackers accessed a university test environment. The affected database contained full names, Danish national identity numbers, work and private telephone numbers, and personal email addresses. The university is still examining the full extent of the exposure. […]

The post University of Copenhagen Data Breach Exposes 525,000 People’s Personal Data, Including Phone Numbers appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The University of Copenhagen has confirmed a data breach that exposed personal information belonging to about 525,000 people after hackers accessed a university test environment.

The affected database contained full names, Danish national identity numbers, work and private telephone numbers, and personal email addresses. The university is still examining the full extent of the exposure.

The attack was detected on October 20, 2026, and publicly disclosed on October 23. According to the university’s official security notice, the university has brought the incident under control and blocked the attackers’ access.

According to reports, the October 25 update confirmed the exposure of ID card PINs belonging to around 20,000 staff and students, with no evidence of disrupted university operations.

The university issued replacement codes and confirmed that this finding was part of the original incident, not a separate attack. It delayed announcing the compromised codes until it changed them.

University of Copenhagen Data Breach Exposes

The university restricted access to selected critical campus locations on October 23, reopening them after replacing affected PIN codes, as the investigation expanded to physical access control data.

The university should not add the 20,000 affected cardholders to the reported 525,000 people as a separate group. The university described them as affected staff and students within the same incident, rather than announcing a new total.

The confirmed entry point was a test environment. However, the university has not disclosed how the hackers gained access, which software was involved, or whether stolen login details or a software flaw enabled the intrusion. Its statement also does not establish that the hackers downloaded or published every exposed record.

The incident highlights the risks of keeping real personal information in testing systems. A related University of Sydney data breach involved historical personal records stored in an online code library intended for software development. That case similarly placed sensitive information inside a development resource.

A separate Dell test platform breach offers a useful contrast. Dell said its affected demonstration environment mainly contained synthetic data and was separated from customer systems. These cases illustrate why the contents and boundaries of test systems matter when assessing a breach’s impact.

The exposed identity and contact details could support targeted phishing and social engineering. Messages that include a person’s real name or other private details may appear credible, so affected people should independently verify unexpected requests rather than trust the information included in them.

The university has reported the incident to the Danish Data Protection Agency and is keeping other relevant authorities informed. It says the breach falls within the scope of GDPR and continues to investigate its extent. Further updates are expected once investigators establish a clearer picture of what happened and which information was affected.

articles.title: DreamHost Forces Email and FTP Password Resets Following Unexplained Security Incident
articles.description:
DreamHost forced password resets for affected email and FTP/SFTP accounts after an unexplained incident disrupted webmail and File Manager, preventing sign-ins until new credentials are set. DreamHost said the password resets were precautionary but has not disclosed the cause or confirmed data theft. The incident began on October 23, 2026, with File Manager connectivity issues. […]

The post DreamHost Forces Email and FTP Password Resets Following Unexplained Security Incident appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
DreamHost forced password resets for affected email and FTP/SFTP accounts after an unexplained incident disrupted webmail and File Manager, preventing sign-ins until new credentials are set.

DreamHost said the password resets were precautionary but has not disclosed the cause or confirmed data theft. The incident began on October 23, 2026, with File Manager connectivity issues.

Later updates reported webmail errors and expanded the password resets to FTP/SFTP users. By October 26 at 3:35 p.m. PDT, engineers had restored the File Manager. They monitored the fix, but password changes remained required.

DreamHost initially told customers to wait for instructions because password changes made before its reset process finished would be overwritten. On October 24, it confirmed that affected account owners could set new passwords directly through the control panel without waiting for an email.

By October 25 at 9:32 p.m. PDT, DreamHost said all impacted account holders had received instructions. It also fixed a “Failed to edit” error that had prevented some Professional Email customers from changing their passwords.

DreamHost Forces Email and FTP Password Resets

The company’s current status notice says affected mailboxes continue receiving messages even when users cannot access them. FTP and SFTP data also remains stored on its servers. This separates the login disruption from any claim of deleted files or lost incoming email.

Account owners should open panel.dreamhost.com directly and use “Mail > Manage Email” for mailbox passwords or “Websites > SFTP Users & Files” for file access credentials. DreamHost says changes can take up to 15 minutes. Saved passwords in email applications and FTP/SFTP clients must also be updated.

DreamHost also advises checking mailbox forwarding settings and removing unfamiliar or unused entries. New credentials should reach affected users by phone call, secure text, or another private channel rather than through their inaccessible DreamHost mailbox.

The forwarding check deserves attention. Previous reporting on hidden mailbox rules in Microsoft 365 shows how attackers can redirect messages and hide security warnings. DreamHost’s recommendation, however, does not establish that attackers changed forwarding settings during this incident.

Unlike the confirmed GoDaddy hosting breach, the available DreamHost notices do not identify an attacker, malware, an entry point, or a confirmed data theft. Password resets alone do not establish those details.

DreamHost says it will never request passwords by email. Its incident updates instruct customers to visit the control panel directly rather than follow login links in notifications. For now, the key unresolved questions remain the incident’s cause, its scope, and whether any unauthorized access occurred.
