articles.title: Hacker With Limited Skills Used DeepSeek AI to Breach Indian University and Steal Over 5,200 Records
articles.description:
A cybercriminal using the online handle BUGSTER used artificial intelligence tools to support attacks on Indian organizations, including two universities. In one confirmed intrusion, the attacker stole a MongoDB database containing more than 5,200 records, including personal information about students and staff, according to Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42. The researchers did not name the […]

The post Hacker With Limited Skills Used DeepSeek AI to Breach Indian University and Steal Over 5,200 Records appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A cybercriminal using the online handle BUGSTER used artificial intelligence tools to support attacks on Indian organizations, including two universities.

In one confirmed intrusion, the attacker stole a MongoDB database containing more than 5,200 records, including personal information about students and staff, according to Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42. The researchers did not name the universities.

The actor’s setup combined Hermes Agent, an AI assistant framework, with DeepSeek V4 as its reasoning model and Cursor as a coding tool.

Unit 42 said the attacker turned off safety controls and relied on AI-written scripts and reports. The case shows how AI can help a person with limited skills take on tasks that once demanded more experience, though it does not mean the model carried out the activity on its own.

Analysts from Unit 42 identified and investigated the activity by examining the operator’s environment, tools and records.

They found evidence of activity beyond the university intrusions, including credential theft, Wi-Fi password cracking, cryptocurrency research, and plans for phone-service fraud.

Hacker With Limited Skills Used DeepSeek AI

At one university, the actor used AI-assisted research to map an online education platform and its related services. The report described a WordPress site, a learning platform, a student portal and an administration dashboard.

The actor then used the information to try account passwords, and the tool identified one working login. Unit 42 did not say that this activity led to the theft of the 5,200 records; that database came from a separate university intrusion.

In the second case, the actor accessed a public university’s database with an administrator account protected by a weak password. The stolen MongoDB data included student records from diploma, undergraduate and postgraduate programs, as well as faculty information.

The actor’s records also showed details about parts of the university’s cloud and database setup. These incidents show why an exposed service or weak account can have serious effects, even without a newly discovered software flaw.

The activity described by Unit 42 relied on basic tools, information gathered about the targets and access to an administrator account.

Readers following DeepSeek-powered Hermes Agent attacks can compare this case with another report on AI-assisted activity involving the same tools.

AI supported work across several schemes

Unit 42 said the actor used AI-generated reports to organize research and produce scripts. Investigators also found a large credential-scanning toolkit designed to look for exposed secrets, such as cloud keys and private keys in files or logs.

This kind of information can give criminals access to services if an organization has left it unprotected. The actor also built AI profiles for separate tasks. One profile was used to seek advice about VoIP fraud, while another researched phone carriers.

Unit 42 found planning material but no call records or signs that the phone operation had become active. This distinction matters: the report documents preparation and research, not proof that the planned fraud was carried out.

Other activity included an automated process for trying to crack Wi-Fi passwords. Unit 42 said it required a device near the target networks to collect authentication data, suggesting the actor had local access to the locations.

The actor also collected information about large cryptocurrency holders, but researchers did not find evidence of follow-up activity against them.

Related reporting on DeepSeek safety research findings covers concerns about AI models producing harmful guidance. Unit 42’s findings add a different point: an attacker can combine an AI model with ordinary tools and weak account security to pursue several types of crime.

Universities and other organizations should review administrator accounts, remove weak or reused passwords, and require multi-factor authentication where possible.

They should also limit database access to approved systems and users, check internet-facing portals for unnecessary exposure, and monitor account activity for unusual login attempts or access to large sets of records.

Organizations should protect secrets such as API keys and cloud credentials by keeping them out of public files and logs. If a credential may have been exposed, teams should revoke or rotate it, then review access records for signs of misuse.

These steps address the security gaps described in the report; they do not depend on identifying a particular AI model. The activity also highlights the value of monitoring what AI agents can access.

If AI tools are used for legitimate work, organizations should limit their permissions, keep safety and approval controls enabled, and review their actions. The case is part of a wider set of reported concerns about AI-enabled cybercrime, including DeepSeek-powered credential theft activity.

articles.title: Oracle Issues Emergency Java Update for Critical 9.1 HTTPS Trust Vulnerability
articles.description:
Oracle has released an emergency Java security update to address CVE-2026-91403, a critical vulnerability affecting how Java applications trust digital certificates. Published on October 21, 2026, the alert assigns the flaw a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.1 and covers Oracle Java SE and GraalVM. The update blocks affected intermediate certificate authority certificates linked to eMudhra. […]

The post Oracle Issues Emergency Java Update for Critical 9.1 HTTPS Trust Vulnerability appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Oracle has released an emergency Java security update to address CVE-2026-91403, a critical vulnerability affecting how Java applications trust digital certificates. Published on October 21, 2026, the alert assigns the flaw a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.1 and covers Oracle Java SE and GraalVM. The update blocks affected intermediate certificate authority certificates linked to eMudhra.

According to Oracle’s security advisory, the issue affects the Java Secure Socket Extension, or JSSE, component. Oracle rates exploitation as low complexity, with no authentication or user interaction required. Successful attacks can expose or change sensitive data, although the risk matrix lists no availability impact.

The problem involves certificate chains that Java uses to decide whether a remote service is trusted. Red Hat explains that eMudhra issued intermediate certificates with weak private keys. An attacker positioned between a Java client and a server could use those weak keys to create certificates for arbitrary hostnames, making a malicious site appear trusted.

This undermines the identity checks behind HTTPS. Encryption alone cannot protect a connection when the client accepts an attacker’s certificate as valid. The fix therefore changes which certificates Java accepts, rather than removing HTTPS support or replacing the entire certificate system. Oracle’s update specifically distrusts the impacted intermediate certificates.

Affected Java and GraalVM Versions

Oracle lists Java SE 8u511, 8u511-perf, 11.0.33, 17.0.21, 21.0.13, 25.0.5, and 27.0.1 as affected. GraalVM for JDK 17.0.21 and 21.0.13, alongside GraalVM Enterprise Edition 21.3.20, are also included. Earlier releases may be vulnerable, but unsupported versions were not tested.

Oracle notes that affected APIs can be reached through services supplying data to JSSE. Its advisory also covers certain sandboxed Java Web Start applications and applets that load untrusted code. The announcement does not report confirmed attacks exploiting this vulnerability.

Oracle recommends installing the latest Java update or following its eMudhra mitigation instructions. Teams unable to update immediately can replace the local blocked.certs file with Oracle’s supplied version, preserving existing custom entries. Java 8 requires the replacement file to be named blacklisted.certs.

Alternatively, Oracle advises enabling TLS revocation checks using -Dcom.sun.net.ssl.checkRevocation=true and -Dcom.sun.security.enableCRLDP=true. For signed JAR verification on JDK 17 and later, it provides jarsigner -verify -revcheck -strict [SIGNED_JAR]. These are alternatives, not steps that must all be applied together.

The emergency alert follows Oracle’s wider patching efforts, including its September security update and August security patches. However, administrators should check this specific advisory rather than assume earlier updates cover the certificate issue. Oracle directs customers to its patch availability document for installation details and recommends moving unsupported deployments to supported releases.

This alleged data theft includes human resources records, training materials, and internal documents. However, the claims are unverified, and PwC has not yet responded. The group’s listing was reported on October 22, 2026. Hackmanac’s public alert […]

The post PwC Data Breach Claim – Everest Ransomware Group Claims to Have Stolen 590 GB of Data appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The Everest ransomware group claims to have stolen 590.69 GB of data from PwC, the global professional services firm. This alleged data theft includes human resources records, training materials, and internal documents. However, the claims are unverified, and PwC has not yet responded.

The group’s listing was reported on October 22, 2026. Hackmanac’s public alert described 108,426 files allegedly taken from internal HR and learning systems. Separately, CTIWatch’s victim tracker recorded PwC appearing on Everest’s leak site that day. These reports document the claim, not independent proof of a breach.

Alleged PwC Data Breach

The supplied leak-site screenshot names a directory, pwc-stg.csod.com, and describes Cornerstone OnDemand platform materials, regional HR exports, e-learning courses, and integration testing documents. It lists 494 directories, alongside 1,333 original archive containers and 53 nested containers. The screenshot alone does not establish how these materials were obtained.

Hackmanac reported that the alleged data spans PwC operations in Australia, China, Canada, and the UK. One HR dataset reportedly contains 213,084 records. That figure should not be read as a confirmed count of affected employees because the number of unique people remains unknown.

The alert also mentions employee information, employment and training records, internal audit methods, confidential documents, and single sign-on source code and configuration files. It does not establish whether working passwords, tokens, or other usable secrets are present.

The screenshot threatens publication after a countdown and urges the company to make contact. A reported October 28 release deadline has not been independently confirmed. No ransom amount, initial access method, or evidence of encrypted PwC systems has been established in the reviewed material.

Everest has previously used data theft claims to pressure named organizations, including its alleged McDonald’s India breach. However, its history includes both data extortion and file encryption, so this listing should not automatically be treated as proof of ransomware deployment.

A separate technical analysis of Everest ransomware found no data theft function inside one examined encryptor. Researchers noted that any theft could instead occur earlier through separate tools. That finding does not explain this alleged incident.

If authentic, detailed employee records could help criminals craft convincing phishing messages or impersonate staff. For now, the central questions remain data authenticity, ownership, access scope, and whether any records are current.

articles.description:
Cisco has released security updates for a critical Cisco Expressway vulnerability that could let remote attackers run operating system commands as root. Tracked as CVE-2026-76466, the flaw carries a CVSS score of 9.8 and affects vulnerable Expressway devices configured in a cluster. Cisco published its advisory on October 21, 2026. The issue affects Cisco Expressway […]

The post Critical Cisco Expressway Vulnerability Enables Remote Code Execution Attacks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Cisco has released security updates for a critical Cisco Expressway vulnerability that could let remote attackers run operating system commands as root.

Tracked as CVE-2026-76466, the flaw carries a CVSS score of 9.8 and affects vulnerable Expressway devices configured in a cluster. Cisco published its advisory on October 21, 2026.

The issue affects Cisco Expressway Core (Expressway-C) and Cisco Expressway Edge (Expressway-E). Both virtual deployments and hardware appliances are affected when running vulnerable software with clustering enabled. Successful exploitation could give attackers control over the underlying operating system.

According to Cisco’s security advisory, the weakness sits in the database service and involves persistent cookies. Cisco also found that client certificates are not properly checked when clustering enables TLS Verify Mode. This means the enabled setting does not provide the expected certificate validation.

An attacker who has the required cookies and network access to an affected device could connect to its database service and invoke specific remote procedure call commands. These calls could allow the attacker to run commands with root privileges, the highest level of access on the system.

Cisco Expressway Vulnerability

Although Cisco describes the attacker as unauthenticated, possession of the cookies remains an important requirement. The advisory does not explain how an attacker would obtain them.

Readers should therefore avoid interpreting the finding as proof that an attacker can immediately compromise every reachable Expressway device.

The potential impact resembles other cases covered in Cyber Security News’ reporting on critical Cisco remote code execution flaws, though the affected products and attack methods differ.

Cisco lists Expressway X15.5.3 and earlier as affected, with X15.5.20 identified as the first fixed release. Customers using X14 or earlier must migrate to a fixed release. No workarounds address this vulnerability.

The fix is also included in Cisco’s broader October 2026 Expressway security hardening release. That release addresses additional weaknesses discovered during an internal security review.

Unlike this cluster-specific flaw, the broader hardening advisory covers affected Expressway-C and Expressway-E devices regardless of configuration. Administrators should check installed versions and cluster settings, then plan upgrades using Cisco’s compatibility guidance.

Checking the version alone does not establish exposure because this particular vulnerability also requires a clustered deployment. Broader coverage is available through Cyber Security News’ Cisco security updates.

Cisco credited Stefan Aleksic of Jane Street with reporting the vulnerability. At publication, its Product Security Incident Response Team said it was unaware of public announcements or malicious use. That statement does not reduce the need to patch affected clusters, given the potential for remote commands to run as root.

The post Splunk Fixes 24 Security Flaws, Including Four Critical Vulnerabilities in Enterprise and SOAR appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Splunk has released security updates for 24 vulnerabilities in Splunk Enterprise and Splunk SOAR, including four critical flaws with CVSS scores from 9.3 to 9.9.

Splunk published the fixes on October 21, 2026, across three advisories covering access control, input handling, exposed files, remote code execution, denial of service, and weak authorization checks.

The Splunk Enterprise security hardening advisory covers four CVEs found internally. CVE-2026-76299 and CVE-2026-76302 both have a 9.9 score and involve improper access control and improper neutralization.

CVE-2026-76300, scored 8.8, concerns poor control of a resource during its lifetime, while CVE-2026-76301 carries a 7.6 score for a protection failure. Splunk groups internal findings by weakness type so that each CVE may represent more than one related issue.

The Splunk SOAR advisory lists eight CVEs fixed in version 8.7.0. The most serious is CVE-2026-76531, rated 9.9, which may leave files or directories open to outside parties.

CVE-2026-76407 is another critical issue with a 9.3 score and involves improper access control. Other SOAR flaws include unsafe URL path checks, poor input handling, weak resource controls, and protection failures.

Critical Severity :

Splunk Fixes 24 Security Flaws

A separate Splunk Enterprise advisory details 12 more flaws, led by CVE-2026-76291 and CVE-2026-76298 at 8.8. The first could let a user with scheduled-search rights bypass safeguards and run risky SPL commands.

The second could allow a low-privileged user to derive the PostgreSQL sidecar superuser password and run operating system commands on search head cluster members.

CVE-2026-76293 also creates a remote code execution risk. A user with the edit_manager_xml capability could run operating system commands through Splunk Web Manager XML.

High Severity :

Two unauthenticated denial-of-service bugs, CVE-2026-76288 and CVE-2026-76290, could make Splunk services stop responding through crafted web requests or repeated package downloads.

The remaining issues affect REST API authorization, field extraction management, sourcetype renaming, SPL filtering, and federated search actions.

Because Splunk often sits at the center of security monitoring, a compromised instance could expose logs, weaken detection, or disrupt investigations. Several flaws require an authenticated user with capabilities, but that does not make them harmless.

Stolen accounts, excessive role permissions, and weak internal access rules could provide the access needed. The unauthenticated denial-of-service issues deserve attention on internet-facing systems because they can affect service without an account.

Medium Severity :

Organizations should review exposed interfaces and user roles while scheduling the updates. Administrators should upgrade Splunk Enterprise to 10.4.4, 10.2.8, 10.0.11, or 9.4.16 and move Splunk SOAR to 8.7.0 or later. Splunk also says CVE-2026-76292 and CVE-2026-76295 need Splunk Secure Gateway updates to 3.10.12, 3.9.26, or 3.8.73.

Teams unable to patch at once can reduce exposure by turning off unused Splunk Web, Pipeline Builders, Secure Gateway, or PostgreSQL sidecar features, depending on the flaw.

These steps can affect key functions, so administrators should review dependencies before making changes. Readers can also review earlier Cyber Security News coverage of multiple Splunk Enterprise vulnerabilities and Splunk SOAR security updates for wider patch history and risk context.

The post Quest Diagnostics Hacked – Attackers Accessed the System to Order Tests and View Results appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Quest Diagnostics has disclosed a cyberattack involving unauthorized access to its Quanum LSM system, which healthcare clients use to order laboratory tests and view results. The company discovered the incident on October 21, 2026, and suspended access to the platform while investigating whether patient records were exposed.

The affected service, Quanum Lab Services Manager, supports test ordering, delivery of results, and searches for previous results. In its official incident notice, Quest said its core business operations remained running. The company said the incident had not materially disrupted its ability to serve patients.

Patient Information Accessed

Quest’s public update confirmed that patient health information or personally identifiable information was involved in the unauthorized access. However, investigators were still determining exactly which information was affected. The company had not disclosed how many patients were involved or provided a detailed breakdown of the records accessed.

That distinction matters. Access to a system containing medical records does not establish that every record was stolen. Quest’s statements describe unauthorized access and potentially affected patient records, but do not establish the full scale of any data theft. Claims about specific stolen information therefore remain unconfirmed.

According to its SEC disclosure, Quest started its incident response procedures, brought in outside cybersecurity experts, and notified federal law enforcement. The response includes containing the activity, investigating its scope, and taking corrective steps. Public reporting has not identified the attackers or their entry method.

Providers using direct customer laboratory information system interfaces or electronic medical records can continue placing orders through those connections, which Quest said were unaffected. Suspending Quanum LSM access therefore does not mean all electronic ordering stopped. Quest said it was working to restore access as soon as possible.

The incident follows other breaches involving medical testing services, including the Laboratory Services Cooperative data breach and the LifeLabs cyberattack. Those separate cases offer context, not evidence of a shared attacker.

Quest said it would make legally required notifications as investigators determine which patient information was affected by this latest incident.

articles.title: Critical Unpatched Linux Kernel Flaws Accidentally Disclosed on Public List
articles.description:
Several unpatched Linux-related security flaws were posted to public mailing lists in October, exposing technical details before fixes were ready. The reports, submitted by Trend Micro’s Zero Day Initiative (ZDI), include two critical flaws rated CVSS 9.0 that could let a remote attacker run code on systems using the Linux kernel’s KSMBD file server. Other […]

The post Critical Unpatched Linux Kernel Flaws Accidentally Disclosed on Public List appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Several unpatched Linux-related security flaws were posted to public mailing lists in October, exposing technical details before fixes were ready.

The reports, submitted by Trend Micro’s Zero Day Initiative (ZDI), include two critical flaws rated CVSS 9.0 that could let a remote attacker run code on systems using the Linux kernel’s KSMBD file server. Other reports describe local privilege-escalation and information-disclosure risks.

The reports appeared on public lists, and Linux kernel maintainer Greg Kroah-Hartman questioned why some submissions were sent there without patches.

But the reports credit Trend Micro’s AI scanner, and reporting on the disclosure points to updated kernel guidance that treats AI-found bugs as already public. ZDI had not publicly explained the routing as of October 23, 2026, so it remains unclear whether this was a simple mistake.

Two Critical Flaws Affect KSMBD

The most urgent reports concern KSMBD, an optional SMB file server built into the Linux kernel. It is separate from Samba, the commonly used file-sharing software. That means the reports do not automatically affect Linux systems running Samba alone. The immediate question for operators is whether KSMBD is enabled and serving files.

ZDI-CAN-33774 describes a race condition in KSMBD that could lead to remote code execution. A race condition occurs when the outcome depends on the timing of tasks running at the same time. In this case, the report says that a mismatch in how the server handles queued network requests may lead to memory being read or written beyond its intended limits. ZDI rated the flaw CVSS 9.0.

ZDI-CAN-33549, also rated CVSS 9.0, affects KSMBD’s SMB Direct path. The reported cause is an integer underflow: a size value can wrap around after a subtraction, leaving the program with an incorrect length.

A later memory operation may then exceed its buffer. The issue concerns SMB Direct, which uses RDMA networking, so exposure depends on the server’s configuration and use of that feature. A fix was reportedly present in a development branch intended for Linux 7.5, but that does not mean it was already available in released or distribution kernels.

At the time of reporting, neither critical issue had a named fix in the mainline kernel or its integration tree, and no CVE identifier had been assigned. Kernel changes also need to reach stable and distribution releases before many users can install them. Administrators should therefore check their Linux vendor’s security notices rather than assume that a fix in a development branch has reached their systems.

Four Other Reports Cover Different Components

The remaining reports do not all affect the same part of Linux. ZDI-CAN-33367 involves the skb_zerocopy networking code and may allow a local user to gain higher privileges. Kernel developers had reportedly received a separate report about the same issue the previous week, with a patch expected. ZDI-CAN-34068 concerns an out-of-bounds write in the VMware graphics driver, which could also enable local privilege escalation.

ZDI-CAN-34076 involves an uninitialized resource in the NVMe over Fabrics target code and may expose information. ZDI-CAN-32005, posted a day earlier, is a stack-buffer overflow in ConnMan’s handling of search-domain TCP queries. ConnMan is a network-management service, not a Linux kernel component, so this report should not be described as a kernel flaw.

Start by checking whether KSMBD is active and whether the system needs it. If it is not required, disabling it reduces exposure to the two remote-code-execution reports.

If it is needed, keep file-sharing services away from untrusted networks, review share access, and monitor the Linux distribution’s security updates for fixes. These steps reduce risk but do not replace installing a vendor-approved patch once it becomes available.

The reports also show why public disclosure before a fix can create pressure for maintainers and system operators. Public details can help defenders understand what to check, but they can also give attackers useful information before updates reach users. For context on earlier KSMBD risks, see Cyber Security News’ coverage of a Linux KSMBD remote-code-execution flaw and its report on an AI-assisted discovery in the Linux SMB server.

For ongoing protection, administrators should follow their distribution’s advisories and apply fixes as soon as they are released.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Contern, Luxembourg, October 22nd, 2026, CyberNewswire

Gcore is offering its WAAP Enterprise plan free of charge to any government body or public agency until December 31, 2026.

The offer follows the php2shell vulnerabilities that forced public websites offline across Europe earlier this week.

Gcore WAAP blocks the php2shell attack path (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) by default for all customers. Sites taken offline can be placed behind the service and brought back online while patching continues.

The two PHP vulnerabilities, rated CVSS 9.2, allow unauthenticated remote code execution before any application code runs.

Government portals in the Netherlands, Finland, Denmark, and France, along with hospitals, schools, and commercial sites, were taken offline this week on the advice of CERT-EU and national agencies.

Going offline was the right call while no fix existed. Patching large estates takes days. A filtering layer that blocks the attack pattern lets a site run while that work is done.

If new variants appear, Gcore updates the rule centrally and operators do not need to repeat the patching cycle.

Gcore’s Enterprise plan covers domains and websites, custom rules, IP reputation, bot management, threat intelligence, API security, and SIEM integration. Public-sector organizations can apply here with an official government domain.

articles.title: Major U.S. Banks Detect Unauthorized AI Agents Operating Inside Customer Accounts
articles.description:
Major U.S. banks are detecting third-party AI agents inside customer accounts, raising concerns that automated tools could act beyond the instructions customers give them. Some agents have contacted call centers or appeared to attempt independent actions, according to an Axios report published October 22, citing people familiar with the matter. Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, […]

The post Major U.S. Banks Detect Unauthorized AI Agents Operating Inside Customer Accounts appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Major U.S. banks are detecting third-party AI agents inside customer accounts, raising concerns that automated tools could act beyond the instructions customers give them. Some agents have contacted call centers or appeared to attempt independent actions, according to an Axios report published October 22, citing people familiar with the matter.

Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, JPMorgan Chase and Wells Fargo are among the institutions working to contain these risks. However, the report does not establish that every named bank detected unauthorized agents. Reuters also reported the findings but said it could not immediately verify them.

The reported access generally starts with customers sharing their banking usernames and passwords with an AI assistant. Customers may approve that access, but the bank may not. Axios reported that such arrangements conflict with rules at most banks requiring customers to log in themselves.

That distinction matters. Unauthorized AI access does not automatically mean hackers stole passwords or broke through a bank’s security systems. In these cases, customers may have opened the door themselves, creating a gap between what they allow and what their bank permits.

The concern grows when agents receive permission to make purchases or move money. Bank executives fear that tools with these powers could take steps customers did not intend. Axios described attempted actions and concerns, not confirmed widespread theft or a disclosed total of financial losses.

The central technical problem is linking account activity to clear human intent. A valid login can show that an account was accessed, but banks still need to determine whether the customer, an approved tool, or an agent acting beyond instructions initiated the activity.

Sources told Axios that banks struggle to distinguish between different agents and determine whether their actions follow user directions. Reported contact with call centers adds another challenge because automated activity may extend beyond a bank’s website or mobile app.

Related Cybersecurity News coverage of dormant AI agents retaining credentials shows why ongoing access deserves attention. That separate report, based on Arrakis Security research, found that many inactive agents still held working credentials. It does not establish a connection to the banking incidents, but highlights the broader problem of permissions outlasting active use.

Banks Block Agents and Consider Limited Access

Morgan Stanley has begun blocking third-party agents, according to sources cited by Axios. JPMorgan, Bank of America and Citi are also restricting access. Banks are updating their terms as they respond to tools that their existing account rules were not designed to handle.

The public statements require careful reading. A Morgan Stanley spokesperson told Axios that the bank had not observed “rogue AI agents accessing our platforms.” A Chase spokesperson warned customers not to share usernames and passwords with anyone. Those comments should not be presented as confirmation of successful autonomous account takeovers.

Most banks have approved, or are moving toward, read-only access, Axios reported. This approach lets third-party tools view financial information without making transactions. Banks already support similar connections for services such as Quicken, offering a possible route for useful automation without direct control over funds.

Separate Cybersecurity News reporting on AI-assisted attacks against financial organizations describes criminals using multiple models to support operations. That activity is different from customers granting assistants account access. Keeping those cases separate avoids confusing deliberate cybercrime with unsafe or poorly controlled automation.

For customers, the message is to follow their bank’s access rules and avoid giving banking passwords to outside AI tools. For banks, the challenge extends beyond blocking bots. They need ways to identify agents, limit permissions, and establish when a customer approved an action.

Axios also reported that banks are preparing recovery plans to secure or restore customer access if incidents occur. The emerging issue is not simply whether AI can enter an account, but whether banks can reliably control what happens next.

articles.description:
eMudhra Limited has announced it is exiting the global SSL/TLS certificate business after disclosing weak private keys in eight intermediate certificate authority certificates. The October 22, 2026, decision follows emergency browser protections and growing questions about the company’s certificate issuance controls. eMudhra said its other digital trust services remain unaffected. In its official announcement, the company said […]

The post eMudhra Exits Global SSL/TLS Certificate Business Following the Vulnerability Disclosure appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
eMudhra Limited has announced it is exiting the global SSL/TLS certificate business after disclosing weak private keys in eight intermediate certificate authority certificates. The October 22, 2026, decision follows emergency browser protections and growing questions about the company’s certificate issuance controls. eMudhra said its other digital trust services remain unaffected.

In its official announcement, the company said its board approved the voluntary exit after reviewing the incident and the business outlook. Chairman V. Srinivasan said eMudhra revoked the affected CA certificates within 14 hours of discovery and promptly disclosed the issue.

The company said none of the affected intermediate CAs had issued end-entity certificates, which websites or software publishers use. It also said its infrastructure was not compromised, no data was breached, and all physical and logical security controls remained intact.

Weak Private Keys Triggered Emergency Action

The incident began with an October 17 report from a researcher identified as Wayne. According to Mozilla’s public incident record, the researcher supplied proof of control over eight private keys. Mozilla independently recovered the keys, confirming that their generation process was seriously flawed. Six affected certificates supported TLS, while two supported code signing.

The technical problem was a lack of randomness. CERT-In said the affected P-384 elliptic-curve private keys had values smaller than 256, allowing them to be recovered almost instantly from their public keys. The failure was in key generation, not in the P-384 algorithm itself.

eMudhra’s preliminary explanation pointed to an April 30, 2025, key-generation ceremony. A flawed script used during a key wrap and unwrap step created a second, weak set of keys. Similar key labels then led staff to use those weak keys in certificate signing requests instead of the original strong keys.

As covered in CybersecurityNews’ earlier report on the eMudhra certificate authority compromise, the issue prompted emergency blocking measures. Anyone recovering these keys could potentially issue false certificates. Where affected chains remained trusted, an attacker able to intercept network traffic could impersonate websites or alter communications.

Google and Mozilla blocked the affected TLS keys on October 17. Both also moved toward removing trust in emSign ECC Root CA – G3, protecting clients that do not reliably receive or enforce intermediate certificate revocation information. CERT-In said Chrome’s root-store change was expected to reach relevant devices on October 27.

eMudhra estimated that about 30,000 certificates required migration. Those certificates should not be confused with certificates issued by the eight weak intermediates. CERT-In said public disclosures had not established confirmed malicious exploitation as of October 21.

The response reflects the wider consequences of certificate authority failures, also seen in Google’s removal of two certificate authorities from Chrome. Browser trust decisions can force website operators to replace otherwise valid certificates to keep services accessible.

eMudhra said global SSL/TLS contributes about 1% of its revenue. Rising data sovereignty requirements, compliance costs and competition from free certificate providers have reduced the business’s returns. Srinivasan also argued that social media scrutiny was out of proportion to the segment’s size.

The company plans to keep its G1 RSA roots serving customers during the transition and provide replacement certificates through partners at no cost. Revocation and certificate status services will continue until issued certificates expire or are replaced. It also committed to completing browser-program obligations, including a full root-cause report.

Meanwhile, CERT-In’s advisory urges administrators to update browsers and trust stores, review certificate chains, and replace affected certificates. Teams should also check separate certificate bundles in applications, containers, and network devices, rather than assuming browser updates protect every system.

articles.title: Claude Security Now Scans Repositories Continuously to Find Flaws and Track Fixes
articles.description:
Anthropic has updated Claude Security so it can keep checking connected code repositories as they change, rather than waiting for a person to start each scan. The service also tracks reported vulnerabilities after developers make changes, marks them fixed when a correction is detected, and reopens them if they return. The updated product is in […]

The post Claude Security Now Scans Repositories Continuously to Find Flaws and Track Fixes appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Anthropic has updated Claude Security so it can keep checking connected code repositories as they change, rather than waiting for a person to start each scan.

The service also tracks reported vulnerabilities after developers make changes, marks them fixed when a correction is detected, and reopens them if they return. The updated product is in public beta for Claude Enterprise customers.

Anthropic says thousands of organizations have used Claude Security since its public beta began in April, finding more than one million vulnerabilities. That figure comes from the company and has not been independently confirmed.

The update aims to help security and development teams keep findings closer to the current state of their software, where new code can introduce risks and older fixes can stop working.

Claude Security Continuous Scans

Teams start by creating a project, connecting repositories, and choosing the branches and code areas to scan. The service supports the Claude GitHub app, including GitHub Enterprise Server, and access tokens for GitLab and other Git providers.

It first performs a deep scan to set a baseline. After that, it checks code changes at intervals based on their risk and complexity. Anthropic says there is no fixed scan schedule.

A project can include multiple repositories. This matters because a security problem may involve how two services work together, rather than a flaw in one file. For example, a backend service may trust that a client has already checked user input. Looking across connected code can help Claude Security assess such relationships and trace how data moves through an application.

Anthropic describes the tool as using its Claude models, including Claude Mythos, for security analysis. It says customers do not need access to the Cyber Verification Program to use the product. Findings include a severity rating based on the project’s threat model, an explanation of how the vulnerable code may be reached, and, in some cases, a diagram showing the path through the application.

The company says its updated service builds on an earlier security-scanning effort. Cyber Security News previously reported on Anthropic’s launch of Claude Code Security, which focused on finding and reviewing code flaws. Its coverage of Claude Code vulnerabilities also highlights why teams need to consider security boundaries when AI tools work with project files and development settings.

Finding a problem is only one part of vulnerability management. Teams still need to decide whether a finding applies to their environment, assign it, make a change, and confirm the issue is gone. Claude Security checks open findings against changed code and can mark them fixed when a correction lands, even if the work happened outside Claude Code. If a later scan detects the same issue again, the finding reopens.

The service also lets teams add knowledge that code alone cannot show. A project can include details about how software is deployed, which security rules apply, and what controls already protect a system.

Claude Security generates a threat model from the code, which the team can review and edit. Later scans use that model to help judge which issues matter and how severe they are. This context can reduce attention on risks that the organization has already addressed, though teams still need to check that the information is correct.

To fit existing security work, Anthropic has added an API, webhooks, and an MCP connector for Claude.ai and Claude Code. Teams can use the API to read findings, manage projects, and resolve or reopen issues.

Webhooks can send alerts when new findings appear. The MCP connector lets engineers discuss a finding and work on a fix from a Claude session. Role-based access controls let administrators set who can view projects, review findings, or create projects.

The service remains in beta, so organizations should treat its findings and fix status as useful signals, not a replacement for human review. Anthropic’s help documentation says scan results can vary between runs and that proposed fixes should be reviewed before use.

articles.description:
ScarlettGroup, a newly observed cyber extortion gang, is naming companies on a dark web leak site and using countdown timers to threaten the release of allegedly stolen data. The operation puts public pressure on organizations before their breach claims have been independently verified. The group began appearing in threat monitoring records around September 2026 and […]

The post A New Extortion Gang Is Naming Companies on the Dark Web and Counting Down to Data Leaks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
ScarlettGroup, a newly observed cyber extortion gang, is naming companies on a dark web leak site and using countdown timers to threaten the release of allegedly stolen data.

The operation puts public pressure on organizations before their breach claims have been independently verified. The group began appearing in threat monitoring records around September 2026 and became more visible during October.

Its listings span technology, education, government, and entertainment, but available evidence does not show a clear focus on one industry or confirm the scale of its activity.

Researchers from Foresiet documented ScarlettGroup’s activity in a report published on October 21, 2026. Foresiet’s threat intelligence research describes an emerging extortion operation, not a confirmed malware family. The researchers have not established how the attackers gain access or whether they deploy ransomware that encrypts files.

A New Extortion Gang Is Naming Companies on the Dark Web

ScarlettGroup’s Tor leak site displays alleged victims alongside publication dates, industry labels, disclosure status, and countdown timers. These details turn an unverified breach claim into a visible deadline.

The aim appears to be pushing targeted organizations toward contact before the group releases the information it claims to hold.

The approach resembles pressure seen in Everest’s alleged BMW breach, where a leak site countdown accompanied claims about stolen internal records.

That comparison concerns the public pressure tactic only; it does not establish any connection between Everest and ScarlettGroup or prove either group’s claims.

ScarlettGroup describes a process with three stages: public listing, a negotiation window, and closure or disclosure. During negotiations, an organization can communicate with the operators.

The group claims a settlement leads to removal of the listing and deletion of the data, while failure to settle may trigger publication. Those promises remain claims made by criminals.

Foresiet notes there is no independent guarantee that information will be deleted after a settlement. A removed listing therefore should not be treated as proof that copies no longer exist or that any possible network access has ended.

What Researchers Have Actually Observed

Foresiet documented ScarlettGroup activity on PwnForums, including alleged breach announcements and data offerings. Reported links involving BreachForums and DarkForums still require verification.

Forum posts can spread allegations beyond a single leak site, increasing attention while also giving defenders leads for further checks.

The lack of confirmed encryption is important. In the separate PAYLOAD attack without encryption, attackers used Windows domain policies and stolen data to create pressure.

ScarlettGroup’s known activity is different: its public threats are documented, but comparable technical details about its intrusion methods have not been established.

The report does not identify an exploited vulnerability, a malware payload, or a verified route into victim networks. It also provides no confirmed victim count.

Treating those gaps as evidence of a particular attack method would go beyond the findings and could mislead security teams investigating an alert.

Foresiet recommends checking criminal claims against independent evidence, preserving forensic material, and monitoring unusual downloads and data transfers.

A company named on the site should investigate possible unauthorized access without presenting the listing itself as confirmation that a breach occurred.

Access controls remain central to prevention. Coverage of Pink’s cloud credential theft shows how another extortion operation targeted accounts and cloud files.

That case is separate from ScarlettGroup, but it underlines the value of Foresiet’s advice to strengthen multifactor authentication, limit account permissions, and review exposed credentials.

Organizations should also assess internet facing systems and keep incident response procedures ready. Monitoring leak sites and underground discussions can help identify claims early, but useful intelligence requires context.

The priority is to establish what happened, which information may be affected, and whether unauthorized activity is continuing. For now, the clearest evidence concerns the gang’s public extortion process, not its tools.

That distinction matters for defenders: a timer can force urgent decisions, but it cannot establish the origin, age, or ownership of the advertised records.

Investigators need evidence from their own systems before judging the claim’s scope or linking it to a wider security incident and planning a response. The deadline itself is not forensic evidence.

articles.title: Hackers Were Targeting Critical PHP Vulnerabilities Days Before They Were Patched
articles.description:
A threat actor tried to exploit two critical PHP vulnerabilities four days before the flaws were publicly disclosed and patched, according to Amazon Threat Intelligence. The activity began on October 17, 2026, while the vulnerabilities were still under coordinated disclosure. The flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and known together as PHP2Shell, can allow remote […]

The post Hackers Were Targeting Critical PHP Vulnerabilities Days Before They Were Patched appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A threat actor tried to exploit two critical PHP vulnerabilities four days before the flaws were publicly disclosed and patched, according to Amazon Threat Intelligence.

The activity began on October 17, 2026, while the vulnerabilities were still under coordinated disclosure. The flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and known together as PHP2Shell, can allow remote code execution on affected web servers.

The early attempt was recorded by MadPot, Amazon’s network of honeypots—systems designed to attract and observe suspicious activity. It came from an IP address linked to a commercial anonymization service.

AWS said it is not clear how the actor obtained information about the vulnerabilities before disclosure, or whether the attempt would have succeeded against a real server.

Analysts from AWS also observed several more PHP2Shell attempts on October 21, before the public release of the fixes. The first proof-of-concept activity appeared around 02:00 UTC, about 12 hours before the disclosure window opened at 14:00 UTC.

The activity used different payloads and anonymized infrastructure, which AWS said may indicate several actors. Additional proof-of-concept exploits appeared after disclosure, and AWS reported that PHP2Shell was being widely exploited.

Hackers Were Targeting Critical PHP Vulnerabilities Days

The vulnerabilities affect PHP’s handling of memory and request data. CVE-2026-109618 is tied to an out-of-memory condition that can leave internal data in an incomplete state.

CVE-2026-109619 involves stale state that may remain in a long-running PHP worker and be used during a later request. In some cases, attackers may be able to use these flaws to run code remotely, without first logging in.

The PHP security team released fixes on October 21. Patched versions include PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12. Older PHP branches may also need vendor-provided updates or an upgrade to a supported release.

Teams should check the specific package or distribution they use, as some vendors may backport a fix without changing the version number shown by the upstream PHP project.

Cybersecurity News previously covered the PHP team’s emergency patch warning, which urged administrators to prepare for the release.

A later report detailed the emergency PHP2Shell security updates. The reports describe separate stages of the same story: the advance warning, followed by the patches for the two flaws.

Why the early activity matters

A patch release does not mark the start of risk. Attackers may learn about a weakness before public disclosure, as AWS’s October 17 observation suggests.

After a fix is published, other attackers can also study the changes and develop working tools quickly. AWS said proof-of-concept exploits appeared within hours of disclosure and urged defenders not to treat the public announcement date as the earliest possible date of exploitation.

That means teams should review activity from before the patch date, not just investigate alerts generated afterward. AWS recommends starting the review from at least October 17.

Relevant checks include web server logs, unusual process launches and unexpected file changes on PHP hosts. Administrators should also look for POST requests containing the string PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS in form uploads.

Organizations should update PHP runtimes as soon as possible and confirm that production workers are running the fixed code.

This includes checking web servers, containers and managed hosting environments, rather than relying only on the PHP version installed for command-line use. A restart or redeployment may be needed so long-running workers stop using the old runtime.

If an immediate update is not possible, AWS suggests considering restrictions on multi-part file uploads. Such a change may affect normal application functions, so teams should assess the impact before applying it.

AWS says configuration-only changes do not fully fix both vulnerabilities; upgrading to a fixed version is the complete remediation.

For more context on reports of activity before the patch, see Cybersecurity News’ coverage of early PHP2Shell exploitation attempts.

Another report covers the public PHP2Shell testing tool. Together, these reports underline why defenders should use multiple signals and avoid depending on a single CVE-specific detection rule.

The provider […]

The post Hackers Planted Malware on Japanese Cloud Servers, Forcing the Provider to Shut Down Its Service appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers planted malware in customer server environments at Japan’s Onamae.com Desktop Cloud, prompting the provider to begin shutting down servers across every service plan.

The company listed 26,739 servers as potentially affected, raising concerns about stored data and login details. That figure describes the possible scope, not a confirmed count of infected systems.

The provider confirmed the malicious programs on October 20, 2026, and began stopping customer servers from 4:00 a.m. Japan time on October 21.

Its official incident notice said the shutdown aimed to prevent further damage. The notice gave no restart date, leaving customers without access while the investigation continued.

Onamae identified the malware in some customer server environments and warned that information held inside those systems may have been viewed.

However, its public findings do not name the malware, explain its functions, or describe how the attackers first gained access. The disclosure confirms an intrusion but leaves the attack chain unresolved.

Hackers Planted Malware on Japanese Cloud Servers, Forcing the Provider

The shutdown covers all Onamae.com Desktop Cloud plans, rather than only the servers where malicious programs were confirmed. Customers cannot use the service while their servers are stopped.

The response recalls the ShareFile emergency server shutdown warning, although that separate case involved a precautionary response to a threat rather than this confirmed malware discovery.

For customers, the immediate problem combines lost access with uncertainty about information stored on their rented servers. Onamae has not publicly identified the affected files, accounts, or applications.

It also has not said whether attackers copied data elsewhere. Possible viewing of information should therefore not be reported as confirmed data theft.

The company said it had found no confirmed leak of the customer personal information it holds, and no confirmed misuse of information that may have been viewed.

It separately stated that it does not retain payment information, including credit card details. These statements do not remove the warning about data inside customer servers.

Technical Details Remain Limited

Onamae has not disclosed an entry point, a security flaw, or a named attacker. Its notice also does not establish whether the malicious programs stole passwords, opened remote access, or performed another task.

Calling the incident ransomware, a supply chain attack, or a campaign by a known group would go beyond the available evidence.

Cloud malware can target secrets stored within hosted systems. In a separate case, reporting on cloud server credential theft described malware built to collect cloud access details.

That example explains the wider concern around server compromise, but it provides no evidence that the same tools or attackers were involved at Onamae.

The provider’s request to change login details makes credential exposure an immediate concern, even without a published malware analysis.

It specifically asked customers to change authentication information stored or used on the servers. That instruction covers a potential route to further account access, not proof that every saved password was stolen.

Users should follow Onamae’s instruction to replace exposed login details promptly and change matching passwords on other services.

The separate ConnectWise backup credential breach showed how a compromised vendor secret enabled unauthorized access across customer environments. The comparison highlights why access details matter; it does not establish how this incident began.

Onamae also warned about phishing emails and suspicious messages exploiting the incident. The company said it would never request passwords or credit card information by email or telephone.

Customers facing an outage should treat such requests with care, especially when a message claims that sharing account information is necessary to restore access.

Security-themed messages can themselves become an entry point. Reporting on passkey themed phishing attacks described criminals posing as support staff to capture cloud access.

Onamae’s warning is preventive: its notice does not confirm that a related phishing campaign has already targeted customers.

articles.title: North Korean Hackers Use Post-Quantum Encryption to Hide New Malware From Security Tools
articles.description:
North Korean-linked Lazarus hackers are using post-quantum cryptography in a malware delivery chain designed to conceal later-stage payloads from security tools. The technique appeared in Operation FlashHole, a campaign targeting organizations in South Korea. Instead of relying on encryption alone to hide files on disk, the malware uses a modern key-establishment method to protect payloads […]

The post North Korean Hackers Use Post-Quantum Encryption to Hide New Malware From Security Tools appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
North Korean-linked Lazarus hackers are using post-quantum cryptography in a malware delivery chain designed to conceal later-stage payloads from security tools.

The technique appeared in Operation FlashHole, a campaign targeting organizations in South Korea. Instead of relying on encryption alone to hide files on disk, the malware uses a modern key-establishment method to protect payloads sent from its command-and-control infrastructure.

The campaign’s infection chain combines phishing, trusted South Korean software, several malware families and code that runs mainly in memory.

At least three organizations in the software, construction and wired communications equipment sectors were affected, according to Kaspersky’s investigation. The researchers say the operation’s earliest known evidence dates to July 2025.

Analysts from Securelist identified the malware and named the activity Operation FlashHole. Their report describes Lazarus abusing CrossWeb EX, a financial security program used to access some South Korean banking and government websites.

Securelist could not confirm exactly how the software was abused, but traced the chain to malicious code running under its process.

This echoes earlier Lazarus activity involving South Korean security software and software supply chains. For more background, see this report on Lazarus malware in supply chains.

North Korean Hackers Use Post-Quantum Encryption

The campaign likely began with targeted phishing emails that directed victims to tailored websites, including fake résumé or interior-design pages.

Securelist found malicious links embedded in these sites and assessed that visiting them may have started the infection process. The researchers also noted signs that an image on one résumé page may have been generated using AI.

They could not confirm every step of the initial compromise, so the precise role of each lure remains an assessment rather than a proven account.

After initial access, the chain used legitimate Windows software and memory-based execution to limit the traces left on disk. The malware set included TechHub, TouchHub, TouchShift, ClientHub, LPEClient and Cubridge.

TechHub helped deliver later components, while other tools supported persistence, system profiling and payload delivery. Cubridge acted as a central operator, able to load separate modules and plugins instead of relying on one large backdoor.

This modular design matters because it can let attackers deploy only the capabilities needed on a particular device. Securelist describes tools that can collect system and process details, search files, and steal browser data such as stored passwords, cookies, bookmarks and browsing history.

Researchers also found that some components communicated through legitimate platforms such as GitHub, while others used compromised websites or Dropbox.

A previous Lazarus software vendor compromise shows why campaigns involving trusted software and supply chains can affect organizations beyond the first victim.

How the post-quantum encryption fits

The most notable change is in LPEClient, a Lazarus malware family used to profile infected computers and deliver further payloads. In this campaign, LPEClient obtains four ML-KEM-1024 public-key blocks from its command-and-control server.

It uses them to establish shared keys, then sends related ciphertexts back through ClientHub. The resulting keys help protect the next payload during delivery and decryption.

ML-KEM is a key-encapsulation mechanism: it lets two parties establish a shared secret over a public channel, which can then be used with symmetric encryption. NIST standardized the method in FIPS 203 and lists ML-KEM-1024 as one of its parameter sets.

Its use does not mean the attackers have a quantum computer; the method is designed to resist attacks from future quantum computers.

Securelist reports that the malware uses the established keys with Threefish to decrypt a later payload, which is then loaded into memory. The report also describes techniques intended to interfere with security monitoring before that payload runs.

These details show why defenders should not treat post-quantum cryptography as a threat by itself: the concern is its use inside a broader chain that combines stealth, trusted software and staged malware delivery.

Organizations in South Korea should review the use and exposure of financial security software, keep it updated, and investigate unusual child processes or unexpected memory activity from trusted applications.

Security teams can also look for suspicious use of GitHub or Dropbox by systems that do not normally need those services, and correlate endpoint alerts with unusual web traffic. These checks are especially useful when malware runs largely in memory and leaves few files behind.

The wider lesson is that malware defenses need to examine behavior and context, not just known file signatures. Lazarus has combined targeted lures, legitimate software, browser-like network traffic and several layers of encryption.

Earlier reporting on Lazarus targeting drone companies offers another example of how the group uses tailored approaches against different sectors.

Securelist assesses with medium-to-high confidence that FlashHole is connected to the earlier Operation SyncHole campaign, based on similarities in targeting and malware.

articles.title: A Hacker Tried to Turn an AI Chatbot Into a Tool for Attacking Other Servers
articles.description:
An exposed artificial intelligence platform can give an intruder more than a place to send messages. If it connects to stored credentials, company data, or network tools, the platform may also provide a route toward those resources. A recent honeypot investigation shows how an attacker tried to use an AI agent to study real infrastructure […]

The post A Hacker Tried to Turn an AI Chatbot Into a Tool for Attacking Other Servers appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
An exposed artificial intelligence platform can give an intruder more than a place to send messages. If it connects to stored credentials, company data, or network tools, the platform may also provide a route toward those resources.

A recent honeypot investigation shows how an attacker tried to use an AI agent to study real infrastructure and prepare further activity.

The incident involved Flowise, an open-source platform for building AI workflows. In late August 2026, an unauthenticated Flowise honeypot received requests to inspect the service, list its workflows, and retrieve stored credentials.

The honeypot was a decoy, not a live production system; it was designed to record activity without running real system commands or a real language model.

Analysts from Sekoia’s Threat Detection & Research team identified the activity and documented how the intruder moved from basic checks to attempts to misuse the AI agent.

Their report describes an operator who tried to obtain sensitive data and turn the chatbot into an assistant for examining other servers. The Sekoia investigation says the activity mainly abused Flowise features rather than relying on a software flaw.

A Hacker Tried to Turn an AI Chatbot Into a Tool

The attacker first checked whether the Flowise service was available and queried its version and node settings. They then requested lists of chatflows and credentials, followed by requests for details tied to specific credentials.

Those steps could reveal AI service keys and database access details on a poorly protected real installation. The early activity lasted about three minutes, then stopped for just over two hours before a wider scan of the API routes.

The report notes that the behavior resembled unauthenticated access associated with CVE-2024-31621, but says that particular flaw was not exploited in the honeypot.

It was fixed in Flowise 1.6.6 and was included in the report only to describe the observed pattern. Separately, the Flowise vulnerability report covers risks tied to exposed Flowise installations and sensitive credentials.

After testing basic inference requests, the operator tried to rename an existing workflow and create a new one called “System Status.” The new workflow included an HTTP Request node aimed at an external server.

If a similar workflow were executed in a live environment, it could make the Flowise server contact attacker-controlled infrastructure. Sekoia described this as misuse of a legitimate outbound request feature, rather than a confirmed software exploit.

Prompts aimed at the AI agent

The attacker also sent prompts designed to probe the agent’s capabilities. They asked it to reveal its system instructions, use tools, run commands, recall a planted access code, and disclose conversations from other users.

These attempts are examples of prompt injection: instructions crafted to push an AI system away from its intended role or safeguards.

The prompts also tried to reach data connected to a simulated finance chatflow. The attacker claimed to be conducting an authorized audit and asked the agent to query a database and summarize financial records.

Sekoia says the operator later tried to get the agent to perform reconnaissance against a simulated internal host. Because the honeypot did not run a real model or execute system commands, the evidence shows attempts—not successful access to real records or systems.

The activity then shifted toward a real target. The prompts included details about a Nightingale monitoring server, Redis data, and an online gambling platform operating across parts of Asia.

The attacker asked for target analysis and guidance on weaknesses and access paths. Sekoia assessed that the information suggested a Chinese-speaking operator and an interest in the online gambling sector, but said there was not enough evidence to link the activity to a known group.

This case is part of a wider concern about agents that combine natural-language prompts with tools, databases, or cloud permissions. A separate report on AI agents and cloud credentials describes how prompt injection can become more serious when an agent can reach services or secrets.

Research on AI agent traps also examines how untrusted content can affect an agent’s decisions and memory. The key risk is not that a chatbot can answer questions.

It is that an agent may be able to act on its answers by calling tools, making network requests, or reading connected data. A prompt alone should not grant access, but weak authentication, broad permissions, and unrestricted network paths can give an attacker more room to work.

Organizations using Flowise or similar platforms should restrict administrative interfaces to authorized users and networks, review who can read or change workflows, and store only the credentials each agent needs.

Teams should also limit outbound connections, monitor unusual requests to workflow and credential APIs, and require human approval before an agent takes actions with sensitive impact. Sekoia recommends strong authentication, strict permission boundaries, and monitoring for prompt injection and misuse of agent capabilities.

articles.title: New Android Malware Replaces Legitimate Banking Apps With Malicious Copies to Bypass Security Checks
articles.description:
A newly identified Android banking Trojan called Hirudo takes an unusual route to financial fraud: it tries to remove a victim’s genuine banking app and install a modified copy in its place. The replacement keeps the bank app’s name and version, but contains extra code designed to interfere with security checks. Instead of relying only […]

The post New Android Malware Replaces Legitimate Banking Apps With Malicious Copies to Bypass Security Checks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A newly identified Android banking Trojan called Hirudo takes an unusual route to financial fraud: it tries to remove a victim’s genuine banking app and install a modified copy in its place.

The replacement keeps the bank app’s name and version, but contains extra code designed to interfere with security checks.

Instead of relying only on fake login screens displayed over a real app, Hirudo’s operators try to make the banking app itself return answers that hide the malware’s presence.

The campaign combines app replacement with credential theft and remote control of infected phones. Its operators can seek banking passwords, payment PINs, SMS messages and device-unlock details, while also viewing the screen and accessing the cameras.

This makes Hirudo more than a fake banking app: it is a remote access Trojan, or RAT, built to help criminals gather information and act on a compromised device.

Analysts from ThreatFabric identified the malware and reported that it has replacement copies prepared for eight Indonesian banking apps covering seven banks.

The researchers also found a wider set of financial apps in Hirudo’s target list, suggesting the operators built a system that could be adapted beyond those banks.

New Android Malware Replaces Legitimate Banking Apps

Hirudo reaches users through apparently useful shopping and entertainment apps. ThreatFabric described lures themed around shopping, adult video and short dramas, including names such as Shopora, 1V1 X, ZoyaTV and KoiShort.

The lure may show real-looking content, such as a storefront or video catalogue, while quietly checking whether the separate Hirudo payload is already installed.

If it is not, the lure displays a fake update prompt and asks the user to install another app package. That second app carries the Trojan and needs its own permissions before its theft and remote-control features can work.

This two-app setup can make the first download appear less suspicious, while the false update persuades the user to install the more dangerous component. It follows a pattern seen in other Android banking threats, such as TrickMo’s abuse of Accessibility permissions.

Once active, Hirudo uses Android’s Accessibility service to detect a targeted banking app and check its signing certificate. It then displays a false update message, opens the system uninstaller for the genuine app and downloads a bank-specific replacement.

The replacement uses the same package name and version as the original, but it is signed with a public test key rather than the bank’s own key. Android will not accept it as an ordinary update over the bank-signed app, so Hirudo first tries to remove the genuine app.

That step creates an important limit: the user may interrupt the uninstall or refuse to approve the replacement installation. But if the modified app is installed, it can load a hidden hooking engine built on the open-source YAHFA and Dobby frameworks.

A hook changes how an app responds when it checks a function or requests information. Hirudo uses this method to interfere with checks from inside the banking app’s own process.

How the banking app is replaced

The engine can return the bank’s genuine signing certificate instead of revealing the test-key signature. It can report an empty list of enabled Accessibility services, hiding the malware’s control service, and remove the FLAG_SECURE setting that blocks screenshots.

The operators may then view or record banking screens remotely. Hirudo also relays some Play Integrity requests to an operator-controlled server, which can return a result for the modified app to accept.

This is why a seemingly successful integrity check does not always prove an app is genuine. ThreatFabric says the attackers’ bundled attestation keybox was publicly leaked, and at least two certificates in it appear on Google’s revocation list.

Banks should check integrity signals on their own servers, including whether certificates have been revoked, and should not rely on a result produced only on a phone that may already be compromised.

Similar credential-stealing Android campaigns, including RatHat’s use of fake app downloads, show why the initial installation path matters as much as later detection.

Beyond replacing banking apps, Hirudo can present fake payment pages and request login passwords or payment PINs.

It can also collect SMS messages, including messages from selected banks and wallets, and in some builds target screen-lock patterns or other unlock details. Its remote-control features include live screen viewing over WebRTC and sessions using the phone’s front or rear camera.

ThreatFabric found that the eight prepared banking-app replacements focus on Indonesia, while the malware’s code includes credential targets in China, India, Mexico, Morocco and Thailand. The fake checkout feature also carries Malaysian bank and wallet branding.

The researchers reported that backend records collected in August 2026 included thousands of credential entries, device information and financial profiles—evidence of an operation designed to organise stolen data for fraud.

Users should be cautious when an app asks them to install an update from outside the official app store, especially if it also requests Accessibility access without a clear need.

Do not remove a banking app or install a replacement at the request of an unfamiliar app. If a banking app disappears unexpectedly or an unfamiliar app requests broad control of the phone, contact the bank using its official contact details and check the device from a trusted channel.

Banks should combine server-side Play Integrity checks with certificate-revocation checks, behaviour monitoring and transaction-risk controls.

They should treat Accessibility and screenshot signals as supporting evidence, not as reliable proof that an app is safe, because Hirudo can tamper with both.

Monitoring should also cover sensitive actions such as login, password recovery, adding a payment beneficiary and approving a transfer. The broader risk is clear: if malware can alter a banking app, signals generated only inside that app may be under an attacker’s control.
